overall.denominator_note: Win, tie and loss rates use the 275 comparable experiments. Unfinished reviews and noncomparable experiments are excluded.
overall.interpretation_note: Each experiment retains its own metric, threshold and comparison rule. Numerical wins do not imply statistical significance or universal superiority. Do not pool gain percentages across different metrics.

categories.name: Gaussian Process Methods
categories.explanation: Multifidelity models and kernel methods achieve several improvements. Exact forward recovery under a quadratic structure must be distinguished from general inverse-map performance: Paper 44 has one win, one tie and one loss.

categories.name: Space-Filling Designs
categories.explanation: Exact exchanges, structural preservation and broader searches account for the main improvements. Some methods also change the feasible class of the original construction. Paper 83 remains unfinished because its integer program exceeds the available license capacity.

categories.name: Optimization Methods
categories.explanation: Paper 95 has no comparable experiments; Paper 17 is unfinished because the baseline encounters empty feasible rho intervals. An improved acquisition objective does not automatically improve the final evaluation metric.

categories.name: Optimal Designs
categories.explanation: Ties dominate, and some designs already attain the corresponding theoretical bounds. Papers 20, 87 and 89 include noncomparable experiments. Numerical optimality diagnostics do not constitute rigorous global certificates.

categories.name: Minimum Aberration and Related Criteria
categories.explanation: Both construction improvements and computational acceleration produce wins; some design-quality criteria already attain their relevant bounds. Paper 64 primarily compares runtime, not an improved aberration value.

categories.name: Active Learning and Sequential Design
categories.explanation: Paper 29 awaits final review because of fidelity issues in the sequential policy and posterior approximation. Paper 58 has conflicting constraints on splitting small leaves. Local variance reduction does not directly imply better prediction, contour estimation or an entire adaptive policy.

categories.name: Order-of-Addition Designs
categories.explanation: Some complete constructions have exact certificates; guarantees in some applications apply only to the fitted surrogate. Theoretical optimality, empirical prediction and computational efficiency require separate interpretations.

categories.name: Big-Data Subsampling
categories.explanation: Sampling benefits depend on information retention and the risk objective. Paper 1 has no wins, one tie and two losses. Removing difficult observations may discard predictive information; general risk dominance is unproved.

categories.name: Classical Experimental Designs
categories.explanation: The results include exact constructions, projection optimization and runtime improvements from equivalent implementations. Better design quality and faster computation should be interpreted separately.

categories.name: Screening Designs
categories.explanation: Most experiments tie. Conditional thresholds and geometric coverage bounds provide guarantees within their stated scope, not universal dominance in screening power.

theory.scope: Validity refers only to the claims checked. Relative improvement is assessed against the original paper within stated conditions; it is not a claim of field-wide novelty.
theory.guarantee_note: Guarantee counts cover final-reviewed papers, including conditional reviews. A paper can have several labels; the rows cannot be added and do not count all theorems.

blocks.heading: Paper 18: L1 distance bound
blocks.text: For LHD(6,3), row sums and parity tighten the upper bound on minimum L1 distance from 7 to 6. An exact O(n) exchange update also allows faster candidate evaluation. The bound concerns this particular finite instance.

blocks.heading: Paper 85: Hadamard auxiliary quantity
blocks.text: Orthogonality, column sums modulo 4 and an attaining construction establish gamma_32=8, replacing the lower bound 6 available from the original paper. This does not prove that Example 2 is globally optimal among all OA(384,341) of the same size. All four numerical comparisons are ties.

blocks.heading: Paper 49: Efficiency lower bounds
blocks.text: Dual information from continuous design and feasible solutions gives tighter lower bounds on efficiency and quantifies distance from the optimum. The original review still contains 32 uncertified records and retains restrictions on exact symbolic representatives; not every returned design can be regarded as certified.

blocks.heading: Paper 63: Fixed-capacity designs
blocks.text: For an odd number of factors, a closed-form determinant is available. Once block capacities are fixed, the optimal choice follows by comparing vertex-pair positions. Both methods attain the optimum in this design class; all four experiments tie.

blocks.heading: Paper 92: Finite-candidate designs
blocks.text: The four near-optimal efficiency lower bounds are approximately 95.50%, 95.96%, 97.00% and 96.60%. These are global certificates under the specified candidate set and model: lower bounds on efficiency, not exact actual efficiencies.

blocks.heading: Paper 33: Additive kernels
blocks.text: Strict positive definiteness of each component kernel alone does not ensure strict positive definiteness of the additive kernel on joint inputs. A four-point rectangle yields a null direction. The repaired argument needs joint-feature conditions or an appropriate nugget.

blocks.heading: Paper 28: Exact debiasing
blocks.text: The original statement omits the code’s acceptance interval for the estimated contraction factor. With three levels (1,0.95,0.9025) and true limit 0, q=0.95 is recovered exactly, but the code rejects it and retains 0.9025. Exact debiasing therefore needs an acceptance-check condition. Parts of the general error decomposition remain valid.

blocks.heading: Paper 95: A path-length counterexample
blocks.text: On [0,1], use the distance h(r)=r log(e/r). Minkowski dimension is 1, but the shortest path through n equally spaced points has length log(e(n−1)). Dimension alone is therefore insufficient for the original general-metric claim; a covering-growth condition is also needed. This counterexample does not invalidate the Euclidean-box application.

blocks.heading: Paper 100: Spectral cutoff constant
blocks.text: On a compact connected Lie group with a bi-invariant metric, spectral products satisfy the (√a+√b)² bound. A 4Λ-design is therefore sufficient for M=I, improving on the paper’s 14Λ condition. The spectral-product mechanism is already in the literature. This result does not prove that the current design uses the fewest nodes.

blocks.heading: Paper 98: Residual correction
blocks.text: Combining independent randomized surrogate integration with residual correction gives an unbiased estimator under the stated sampling conditions. If the proposal satisfies q≥0.1f, where f is the target density, importance weights are at most 10. The surrogate itself need not be exactly correct.

blocks.heading: Variance comparison
blocks.text: Stratification in probability coordinates does not increase variance relative to iid sampling with the same fixed surrogate and proposal. The comparator is this estimator’s own iid version. The result does not establish uniform superiority over the source paper’s full adaptive algorithm.

blocks.heading: 032, 076 | Attained bounds and restricted optimality
blocks.text: Paper 32’s full-permutation construction attains B = 0 and LC = 2(m!−1) simultaneously; general COA branches do not inherit every optimality property. Paper 76’s occupancy bound certifies the regular subclass; the saturated-size frame bound has a separately defined scope.

blocks.heading: 080, 087 | Valid proofs and performance claims
blocks.text: Paper 80 proves quadratic-slope recovery under the specified reflection and covariance conditions, not complete quadratic prediction; its first experiment also does not retain GOA stratification. Paper 87 proves a model-specific edge reduction, but an observed maximum is not the global upper bound needed for an efficiency certificate.

papers.title: GEMSS-Driven Subsampling for Information Extraction and Redundancy Elimination
papers.short_title: GEMSS-Driven Subsampling for Information Extraction and Redundancy Elimination
original_method: GEMSS uses residual and conditional-variance scores to extract informative observations or delete redundant ones, followed by a validation-selected GP fit.
our_method: Extraction uses a distilled finite-reference risk criterion; elimination uses leave-one-out deletion. Pilot estimation, data splits and downstream fitting are shared.
papers.baseline_implementation: The comparison uses the frozen reconstruction and settings below. Results are actual runs, not numerical values copied from the paper. Fidelity qualifications and source locations remain part of the interpretation.

theory: verified: Fixed-parameter block inverse, observed-nugget LOO variance, finite-reference surrogate gain and leave-two-out identities reviewed in supplement/theory.md; narrow algebraic claims valid. The prior numerical checks corroborate algebra only.

limits: PDF p4 Theorem 1 assumes noise-free conditions; p5 Theorem 2 is about an upper bound for a component and does not establish general test-risk or actual-conditioning superiority. Separate author S1–S4 proof supplement remains unverified.

attribution: Observed LOO-trimming test losses are consistent with the acknowledged risk of discarding difficult informative observations, but this mechanism is an interpretation, not a proven causal explanation.
relative_significance_contribution: Relative significance: Moderate. Relative contribution: Not confirmed. This is an editorial comparison of the recorded original-paper mappings and Judge findings, not a claim of literature-wide novelty or an additional independent Judge session.
Fixed-parameter identities supplement the implementation, but do not establish improved risk or conditioning relative to the paper.

The available record does not establish a stronger final guarantee relative to the original method. Algebraic validity, structural preservation, or an empirical win alone does not establish such a contribution.

papers.title: Bayesian Optimization for Branching and Nested Hyperparameters in Deep Learning
papers.short_title: Noisy Bayesian optimization with branching and nested hyperparameters
papers.authors: Jiazhao Zhang; Chung-Ching Lin; Ying Hung
papers.research_question: Network type, depth and training parameters often have conditional dependencies: some parameters are meaningful only within a particular branch. This paper studies how to model correlation when shared continuous parameters coexist with branch-specific parameters, and how to find good configurations with a limited budget of noisy evaluations.
original_method: The original method uses a Gaussian process to represent shared continuous variables, branch categories and categories nested within each branch. Its covariance combines these components, with different correlation parameters within and across branches. This shares information between configurations while retaining their conditional dependencies; parameters are estimated by constrained likelihood.

Sampling uses expected improvement, with the best current noisy observation as the reference. The paper considers sequential and batch search. Batch search must schedule several candidates before their responses return, so within-batch dependence and delayed feedback affect the actual selections.
our_method: We extend the original product kernel to a positive-weight mixture of six terms representing categorical effects, effects of the two continuous dimensions, and their interactions. We learn the weights from observed responses. Categorical correlations use the exact positive-definiteness conditions for a two-group matrix, allowing a larger feasible region than the original sufficient conditions.

The expected-improvement reference is replaced by an estimate based on the posterior mean, intended to reduce the influence of an unusually noisy best observation. Both methods share the numerical search and within-batch fantasy-observation procedure. The changes are compared jointly; the contributions of kernel mixing and reference denoising are not isolated.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline was reconstructed from the tabulated formulas in the 15-page preprint, using a Matérn kernel and estimated mean and scale. Journal-author code obtained later differs in the signs of function centers, kernel, constraints and batch selection. The present comparison therefore cannot be described as a reproduction of the journal code.

experiments.label: Sequential noisy search
experiments.setup: A synthetic function has two continuous variables, two branches and five valid category combinations, with observation-noise standard deviation 0.2. Each run starts from 10 shared initial points and adds 50 sequential evaluations. The 20 paired repetitions share initial data and noise.
experiments.metric: Best true function value at queried locations
experiments.explanation: The baseline wins. Our method has worse true search quality and greater variability. Its largest noisy observation is nevertheless higher, showing that observed extrema alone can include apparent gains due to noise. For each run, take the best noise-free value among the 60 queried locations, then average over 20 repetitions. True values are not fed back to the methods.

experiments.label: Delayed-feedback search in batches of five
experiments.setup: The same synthetic function, domain and noise level are used. After 10 initial points, each run adds 10 batches of five points. Actual observations return only after the whole batch has been selected. There are 20 paired repetitions, still with 60 calls per run.
experiments.metric: Best true function value at queried locations
experiments.explanation: The baseline wins under the prespecified mean tolerance, but the interval for paired differences crosses zero. papers.title: A New Approach to Optimal Design under Model Uncertainty Motivated by Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.short_title: Sequential information-optimal design under model uncertainty
papers.authors: Mingyao Ai; Holger Dette; Zhengfu Liu; Jun Yu
papers.research_question: When several regression models may explain the response, designing for a single model can select unsuitable sampling locations. The paper incorporates model discrimination and parameter estimation into sequential design, asking how to allocate experiments as data accumulate so that the final design retains high D-efficiency under the true model.
original_method: The original method treats candidate models as arms in a selection problem. It maintains a Beta distribution for each model, randomly selects a currently promising model, and allocates the next batch around its locally D-optimal design. Dose-response settings also mix in a uniform design to retain exploration for model discrimination.

Updates mainly use the current batch's fits, BIC and, where needed, goodness-of-fit tests, rather than always pooling historical data. An inestimable candidate model is not simply treated as a failure. Final D-efficiency is computed from the information matrix of all points actually collected.
our_method: We use cumulative data to form BIC weights and retain a gradually decreasing uniform component, avoiding permanent early exclusion of a model. The next batch directly maximizes the weighted information-determinant increment across candidate models, accounting for information already accumulated.

Integer greedy allocation adds points one at a time within a batch. Whitening by a reference information matrix prevents regularization from changing arbitrarily with parameter units. An objective-gap upper bound is also computed for each batch to assess solution quality on the finite candidate set; it is not an optimality certificate for final efficiency under the true model.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline implements Beta selection, current-batch updating and handling of inestimable models from the 38-page preprint. Both methods use a fixed candidate-design library and integer allocation. The journal supplement differs from this preprint setting in the number of stages, parameters and sample sizes.

experiments.label: Three dose-response models
experiments.setup: Emax, linear and exponential models are compared on the dose domain [0,1]. Two effect strengths and three true models give six scenarios. Noise standard deviation is 0.65; each scenario uses 10 batches of 15 points. Each method runs 100 paired repetitions.
experiments.explanation: The mean efficiency gain is positive in all six scenarios, and our method wins overall. Final BIC discrimination accuracy decreases slightly, however, so higher efficiency does not imply a general improvement in model selection. Within each repetition, average efficiencies equally across the six scenarios, then take the arithmetic mean over 100 repetitions. The denominator is an analytically derived approximate optimal design.

experiments.label: Three-dimensional polynomial model discrimination
experiments.setup: Six candidate polynomial models are retained, with M1, M5 and M6 as the three true-model scenarios. Design uses a 21³ grid, with 15 batches of 36 points per scenario, totaling 540 points. Noise is standard Gaussian; there are 100 paired repetitions.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins, with positive mean gains under all three true models. It uses more support points across stages and more computation, so neither faster execution nor fewer support points can be claimed. Average equally across the three scenarios first, then average over seeds. Singular information matrices receive zero under the scoring rule.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Final BIC discrimination accuracy decreases slightly, however, so higher efficiency does not imply a general improvement in model selection. Within each repetition, average efficiencies equally across the six scenarios, then take the arithmetic mean over 100 repetitions. The denominator is an analytically derived approximate optimal design.

Experiment 2: Our method wins, with positive mean gains under all three true models. It uses more support points across stages and more computation, so neither faster execution nor fewer support points can be claimed. Average equally across the three scenarios first, then average over seeds. Singular information matrices receive zero under the scoring rule.
results_interpretation: Both experiments improve final D-efficiency, supporting the combination of cumulative model information and weighted batch design. Gains do not simultaneously extend to discrimination accuracy, minimum support size or computation time. In particular, the polynomial setting's efficiency gain comes with a higher design-computation cost.
theory: With fixed history, within-batch weights and a finite candidate set, regularized logdet has diminishing returns, yielding a greedy approximation factor and a concavity-based gap certificate. These guarantees concern a single-batch objective; they do not establish global optimality of the full adaptive strategy or on a continuous domain.
limitations: The formal runs use 100 repetitions, fewer than the paper's 500; experimental settings also differ between the preprint and journal supplement. A grid certificate does not establish continuous-domain optimality or globally minimum support.

papers.title: Sequential Latin hypercube design for two-layer computer simulators
papers.short_title: Sequential output-space design for a two-layer simulator
papers.authors: Yan Wang; Dianpeng Wang; Xiaowei Yue
papers.research_question: For a two-layer simulator, a uniform design in the inner simulator's input space need not yield uniformly distributed outputs, which in turn are the outer simulator's inputs. The paper studies how to choose new points when inner responses can only be queried sequentially, and evaluates separation between the final output points.
original_method: The original method begins with a Latin hypercube design, standardizes the observed multivariate outputs and applies principal component analysis, retaining components whose cumulative explained variance strictly exceeds 90%. A separate Gaussian process is fitted to each retained component. Predictive means and variances then define distances between candidate points.

Sequential selection uses a finite-order phi-distance criterion to approximate maximization of the minimum spacing and adds points from sliced Latin candidate designs. Output reduction, surrogate updating and distance optimization are repeated after each observation to adapt to the incompletely known inner mapping.
our_method: We retain the full numerical rank on the original output scale, preventing standardization or principal-component truncation from changing the distances used for scoring here. Candidates are scored by the average distance from their predicted output to existing outputs, with an uncertainty term based on the trace of posterior variance.

This selection objective directly matches the final average pairwise distance, instead of continuing to optimize an approximation to minimum spacing. Both methods use the same initial design, candidate pool and simulator-call count. Full output representation and the new objective change together, so their individual contributions cannot be separated.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline reconstructs sequential PCA, a Matérn surrogate and phi15 selection from the 34-page preprint. Initial and sliced designs are optimized by local exchanges. Author-code defaults and the distance coordinates in the original figures were not verified; scoring here explicitly uses all true, untransformed outputs.

experiments.label: Two Camel outputs with two-dimensional inputs
experiments.setup: Two Camel functions provide outputs on the two-dimensional unit square. After 20 initial points, 100 points are added from 1,000 shared candidates, giving 120 final points. Each method has 10 paired repetitions. An independent 2,000-point probe set evaluates an auxiliary covering radius.
experiments.metric: Mean pairwise distance in raw output space
experiments.explanation: Our method wins on average separation, but its probe-set covering radius increases substantially. Greater concentration at extreme locations does not ensure more uniform coverage of intermediate regions. For each repetition, compute the average distance among the true, unstandardized outputs of the final 120 points, then average over 10 repetitions.

experiments.label: Eight-dimensional inputs and ten correlated outputs
experiments.setup: An eight-dimensional unit cube and fixed coefficients generate ten correlated outputs. After 80 initial points, 360 are added from 14,400 candidates. There are 440 final points and 10 paired repetitions. An independent 2,000-point probe set is used only for post-run coverage evaluation.
experiments.metric: Mean pairwise distance in raw output space
experiments.explanation: Our method wins on the primary metric, while the covering radius worsens, input separation decreases and design computation takes longer. The result supports improvement in the targeted average distance, not in all space-filling properties. Distances use all ten true output dimensions, not PCA scores or outer-layer prediction error.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 2: Our method wins on the primary metric, while the covering radius worsens, input separation decreases and design computation takes longer. results_interpretation: Both experiments increase average pairwise output distance, showing that direct optimization of this metric can yield substantial gains. Auxiliary results reveal tradeoffs in coverage and computational cost. The findings cannot be summarized as a general improvement in spatial coverage or substitute for untested outer-layer prediction accuracy.
theory: The relationship between finite-order phi and minimum spacing, distance preservation in the full subspace, and one-step AID increments can be proved. The implemented uncertainty radii lack simultaneous coverage guarantees over the candidate set, so the associated one-step bounds remain conditional, not operational high-probability optimality guarantees.
limitations: Outer-layer prediction, the assembly application and other initialization ablations were not run. High-dimensional outputs require preservation of their full actual subspace; numerical rank identification and confidence radii remain conditional.

papers.title: Active Learning with Adaptive Non stationary Kernel for Continuous-Fidelity Surrogate Models
papers.short_title: Adaptive kernels and mesh-aware modeling for continuous-fidelity simulation
papers.authors: Romain Boutelet-Smith; Chih-Li Sung
papers.research_question: Numerical simulation error varies with mesh size, and finer simulations are usually more expensive. The paper studies joint selection of physical inputs and continuous fidelity to predict the zero-discretization-error limit under a limited computational budget, while accommodating nonstationary error correlation across fidelities.
original_method: The original model decomposes simulator output into a target response and numerical discretization error, represented by independent Gaussian processes. The error kernel is based on a transformed fractional Brownian covariance, whose parameters control cross-fidelity dependence while the error variance tends to zero with fidelity.

Restricted likelihood estimates spatial scales, error scales and correlation parameters, and prediction retains uncertainty from mean estimation. The next call maximizes the reduction in integrated predictive variance at zero fidelity per unit simulation cost, searching jointly over input location and fidelity.
our_method: The stochastic-process experiment retains the original adaptive kernel and only weakly regularizes hyperparameter fitting. The finite-element experiments additionally replace nominal fidelity by the edge length of the generated mesh, avoiding treatment of nominal inputs that generate the same mesh as different accuracies.

For the spatially averaged response, the error trend is squared mesh edge length times a quadratic spatial polynomial; for the maximum response it is a scalar squared-edge-length trend. Selection also compares costs over nominal intervals corresponding to discrete meshes. Only mesh-generation rules and paid responses are used, not the analytic truth.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline implements the adaptive kernel, REML and cost-adjusted integrated-variance sampling from the 41-page preprint. Initial designs use an MMED variant with a fixed point count. All Poisson runs use triangular P1 finite elements, a declared solver substitution that is not identical to the authors' MATLAB mesh.

experiments.label: Nine continuous-fidelity stochastic processes
experiments.setup: For a one-dimensional input, spatial-scale and correlation parameters form a 3×3 grid. Each scenario has 16 initial points, initial cost 64 and total cost 128; call cost is inverse squared fidelity. There are 10 paired process/design repetitions, with zero-fidelity responses predicted at 501 final evaluation points.
experiments.explanation: Weak regularization produces overall error close to the baseline, giving a tie. Aggregation across the nine generating settings provides no evidence of a general predictive benefit from this fitting change. Average the nine RMSEs within each seed, then average over 10 seeds. These are not 90 independent repetitions.

experiments.label: Spatially averaged Poisson response
experiments.setup: A Poisson equation with zero boundary conditions is solved on a two-dimensional spatial domain, with a one-dimensional physical parameter. The response is an area-weighted finite-element integral. Ten shared initial points cost 500; total cost is 1,500. There are 10 paired repetitions and prediction RMSE is evaluated at 501 points.
experiments.metric: RMSE of the spatially averaged response
experiments.explanation: Our method wins. Mesh correspondence and a squared-error trend provide a plausible explanation for its suitability. The trend, fitting and cost search all change, so the gain cannot be assigned to one component. Arithmetic means of RMSE on the original response scale; unweighted averages of nodal values are not used.

experiments.label: Spatial maximum of the Poisson response
experiments.setup: The same Poisson equation, fidelity interval and budget are used, with the maximum of the piecewise-linear finite-element field as response. Each run has 10 initial points, total cost 1,500 and 10 paired repetitions. The limiting maximum response is predicted on the shared 501-point scoring set.
experiments.metric: RMSE of the spatial maximum response
experiments.explanation: Our method wins, with a smaller improvement than for the spatial average. The theoretical order for finite-element average error cannot be transferred directly to the maximum response; this remains an empirical finding. Arithmetic mean of the 501-point RMSE from each run. This is a different response of the same PDE as the preceding experiment.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 1: Weak regularization produces overall error close to the baseline, giving a tie. Aggregation across the nine generating settings provides no evidence of a general predictive benefit from this fitting change. Average the nine RMSEs within each seed, then average over 10 seeds. These are not 90 independent repetitions.

Experiment 2: Our method wins. Mesh correspondence and a squared-error trend provide a plausible explanation for its suitability. The trend, fitting and cost search all change, so the gain cannot be assigned to one component. Arithmetic means of RMSE on the original response scale; unweighted averages of nodal values are not used.

Experiment 3: Our method wins, with a smaller improvement than for the spatial average. The theoretical order for finite-element average error cannot be transferred directly to the maximum response; this remains an empirical finding. Arithmetic mean of the 501-point RMSE from each run. This is a different response of the same PDE as the preceding experiment.
results_interpretation: The three experiments give two wins and one tie. Regularization alone does not improve average accuracy in the stochastic-process experiment, whereas the mesh-aware model helps for both Poisson responses. The advantages occur at equal simulation cost; our method takes more wall-clock time, so faster execution cannot also be claimed.
theory: There are explicit derivations for kernel positive semidefiniteness, variance reduction at fixed parameters and reproduction of the error trend, and a sign error in the original appendix is corrected. These results do not establish monotonicity of integrated error after refitting, function-space membership of the actual finite-element residual, or the error order of the maximum response.

papers.title: Efficient Active Learning Strategies for Computer Experiments
papers.short_title: Predictive sampling and optimization with a mixed additive kernel
papers.authors: Difan Song; V. Roshan Joseph
papers.research_question: In high-dimensional computer experiments, some inputs may be inactive while some responses contain substantial interactions. This paper studies initialization and sequential sampling that combine variable exploration with surrogate modeling, separately considering prediction of unknown responses and minimization of a function.
original_method: The original method initializes with a maximum one-factor-at-a-time design, allowing a limited number of points to explore changes in each input. It then fits a Gaussian process with a product inverse-multiquadric kernel. Dimension-specific length scales and a shared shape parameter are estimated by likelihood to adapt to the relevance of different inputs.

For prediction, maximum posterior variance selects uncertain locations; for optimization, expected improvement balances exploration and exploitation around the smallest observed value. The model is updated after each response until the prescribed total number of function calls is reached.
our_method: We combine an additive squared-exponential kernel with learned weights and a full-product residual kernel, allowing both low-order structure and interactions. All experiments use the same model form; the true active inputs and objective structure are not supplied to the method.

Prediction uses integrated variance reduction on a finite reference set, with the maximum-variance candidate from the same model included in the comparison. Optimization retains expected improvement. Thus prediction changes both kernel and sampling criterion, whereas optimization mainly changes the fitted model and its induced trajectory.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline reproduces MOFAT initialization, MIM fitting and ALM/EI from the 28-page preprint. Subsequent official code uses different initialization, parameter ranges, update frequency and experiment sizes, and adds a sensitivity-weighted branch. That integrated journal-version method was not run here.

experiments.label: Friedman prediction with inactive inputs
experiments.setup: Only five inputs affect the Friedman response in a ten-dimensional unit cube. Both methods share a 44-point initial design and sequentially reach 100 noise-free calls. Ten paired repetitions are evaluated on 1,000 Sobol points generated after learning ends.
experiments.explanation: Mean MSE meets the criterion for our method to win, but the paired interval crosses zero. Compatibility between low-order structure and the additive kernel is a plausible explanation; model and sampling contributions cannot be separated. Arithmetic mean of MSE on the original scale, not RMSE or a log-transformed quantity.

experiments.label: Ten-variable wing-weight prediction
experiments.setup: The ten-dimensional unit cube is mapped to the original wing-weight model's engineering parameter ranges, retaining all inputs and interactions. Each run has 44 initial points and 100 noise-free calls in total. Ten paired repetitions use a shared 1,000-point test set.
experiments.explanation: The baseline wins. The present mixed-kernel/integrated-variance combination does not outperform MIM with maximum-variance sampling. The paired interval crosses zero, so deterioration cannot be attributed conclusively to the interaction structure. Compute MSE in the original weight units, then average over 10 repetitions.

experiments.label: Six-dimensional Levy optimization
experiments.setup: The noise-free Levy function is searched on [-10,10] in six dimensions. A shared 28-point initialization is extended to 90 calls, with 10 paired repetitions. The primary metric is the smallest queried function value minus the known global minimum zero; the optimum location is used only for scoring.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins and every paired repetition improves, providing the clearest gain among the four experiments. Both methods retain the same expected-improvement rule, but kernel form and fitting settings are still not isolated. Arithmetic mean of endpoint regret, not cumulative regret or a trajectory average.

experiments.label: Levy optimization with four additional inactive inputs
experiments.setup: The first six variables still determine the Levy response, but the methods receive ten inputs without being told which are inactive. A 44-point initialization is extended to 150 calls, with 10 paired repetitions. The budget is based on total dimension; this is not a Levy problem with ten active variables.
experiments.explanation: Mean regret meets the win criterion, but the paired interval crosses zero and variability is substantial. Learning variable contributions may help, but a stable advantage with inactive inputs is not established. Subtract zero from the smallest value among each run's 150 actual queries, then average over repetitions.

papers.title: Multi-Layer Sliced Design and Analysis with Application to AI Assurance
papers.short_title: Identifiable effect estimation in multilayer sliced designs
papers.authors: Qing Guo; Xinwei Deng; Peter Chien
papers.research_question: Multilayer sliced designs compare platform configurations and design factors jointly, but conditional effects and design-factor-by-slice interactions can be exactly linearly redundant. The paper examines slice main-effect estimation in fixed two-layer and three-layer designs, comparing errors from sparse shrinkage and identifiable parameterization.
intro_notes: Classification: the report retains the initial space-filling category. Full-text review reassigns the primary category to minimum aberration and related criteria.
original_method: The original paper constructs two-level multilayer sliced designs using sliced word-length patterns and minimum-aberration principles, observing all slice combinations. The analysis includes conditional design effects, slice main effects and interactions, allowing factor effects to vary across platform configurations.

Effect estimation uses induced-smoothing Lasso, selects the penalty by AIC, and then sets insignificant coefficients to zero using Wald tests. This supports sparse interpretation, but shrinkage and thresholding can bias target coefficients under redundant parameterization and small samples.
our_method: We keep the original designs and observations, remove duplicate parameter representations through identities among conditional columns, and compute least-squares contrasts in the identifiable orthogonal space of the same mean model. Interaction contributions are absorbed into the relevant conditional slopes, rather than assumed to be zero.

Slice main effects are obtained directly from the orthogonal contrast U^T y/n, without penalty shrinkage or Wald thresholding. The model receives no true coefficients, noise variance or extra observations. The change concerns estimation, not construction of a better experimental design.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline follows the paper and author simulation script for islasso AIC selection, refitting and significance thresholding, using a fixed public package version. The text and script conflict on coefficients and noise settings; data here follow the prespecified coefficients and variances in the main text.

experiments.label: Two-layer, sixteen-run design
experiments.setup: Two layers of slicing factors and three design factors give 16 runs. Both designs d1 and d2 and noise variances 1 and 0.5 are retained. Each seed fits four combinations, with identical responses for both methods. There are 100 paired repetitions, scored by squared error in the two slice main coefficients.
experiments.explanation: Main-effect estimation wins, and prediction and slice-interaction errors also decrease. An empirical decomposition indicates that bias reduction exceeds the variance increase; this decomposition is not a new win criterion. Average the two coefficient errors within each combination, average equally across the four combinations, then average over 100 repetitions.

experiments.label: Three-layer, thirty-two-run design
experiments.setup: Three layers of slicing factors and three design factors give 32 runs. The four combinations of two designs and noise variances 1 and 0.5 are retained. Each method has 100 paired repetitions sharing training responses. The primary metric averages squared errors of the three slice main coefficients.
experiments.explanation: Main effects and signal prediction improve, but error in pairwise slice interactions increases. Retaining interactions that are truly zero increases variance, so improvement in every coefficient estimate cannot be claimed. Average the three main-coefficient errors within a combination, then average equally over four combinations and 100 repetitions.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 1: Main-effect estimation wins, and prediction and slice-interaction errors also decrease. An empirical decomposition indicates that bias reduction exceeds the variance increase; this decomposition is not a new win criterion. Average the two coefficient errors within each combination, average equally across the four combinations, then average over 100 repetitions.

Experiment 2: Main effects and signal prediction improve, but error in pairwise slice interactions increases. Retaining interactions that are truly zero increases variance, so improvement in every coefficient estimate cannot be claimed. Average the three main-coefficient errors within a combination, then average equally over four combinations and 100 repetitions.
results_interpretation: Both experiments reduce slice main-effect error, supporting use of exact design structure to remove unnecessary shrinkage bias. Deterioration in three-layer interaction estimates shows a bias-variance tradeoff. The findings concern simulated analysis on fixed designs, not advantages in design construction or the MNIST application.
theory: Under a correct linear mean and independent homoscedastic Gaussian errors, identifiable orthogonal contrasts are unbiased with variance σ²/n and an exact finite-sample chi-squared risk expression. Optimality among linear unbiased estimators does not imply uniformly smaller MSE than biased Lasso. A saturated model also lacks the usual residual variance estimator.
limitations: The authors' historical package version is unknown, and the low-noise settings differ between the text and code. The MNIST application was not run; conclusions concern simulated estimation on fixed sliced designs.

papers.title: PICS: A Sequential Approach to Obtain Optimal Designs for Nonlinear Models Leveraging Closed-Form Solutions for Faster Convergence
papers.short_title: Sequential sampling using closed-form optimal designs
papers.authors: Suvrojit Ghosh; Koulik Khamaru; Tirthankar Dasgupta
papers.research_question: Optimal designs for nonlinear models depend on unknown parameters, and repeatedly solving design problems numerically adds cost. The paper uses available closed-form optimal designs to schedule new observations as parameter estimates change, comparing random sampling at optimal probabilities with deterministic selection accounting for parameter uncertainty.
original_method: PICS estimates parameters from initial data, substitutes them into closed-form support points and probabilities for a locally optimal design, and randomly draws an experimental point. After each new response, parameters are re-estimated from all historical data. This continues to the sample budget.

The approach replaces repeated design optimization by closed-form calculation and probabilistic sampling. It applies to exponential-linear growth and constrained logistic regression. Balanced PICS already exists in the original paper; the present baseline is the fully sequential randomized version, and existing balanced allocation is not presented as a new method.
our_method: Using current estimates and the information matrix, we build a local uncertainty set along permitted parameter directions and combine its associated closed-form support points. Current PICS support is always included. The optimal design at the true parameters is not supplied.

Given the information from existing observations, we choose the candidate with the largest weighted logdet increment, instead of random sampling at current-parameter probabilities. The set is only a local approximation, not an exact posterior. Deterministic maximization improves the one-step information objective under that same set.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline implements closed-form support, randomized single-point sampling and cumulative refitting from the 30-page preprint. Constrained logistic regression uses parameter ranges supported by the author code. Both methods share the fitter; global optimality of the nonlinear likelihood fit is not proved.

experiments.label: Growth model with an unknown change point
experiments.setup: The same growth model and input interval are used, with the change point also unknown, for three estimated parameters. There are 60 initial and 200 final points, noise variance 0.086 and 50 paired repetitions. Sampling support changes with the current change-point estimate.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins and true D-efficiency improves, but parameter error does not decrease. This supports the information-allocation objective, not gains for every estimation target. The original absolute-deviation score based on the estimated information determinant is retained and averaged arithmetically over repetitions.

experiments.label: Equal-coefficient logistic regression
experiments.setup: A binomial logistic model uses four combinations of two factors, with intercept and both main coefficients constrained to be equal. Twenty-five observations per combination give 100 initial points, followed by sequential sampling to 1,200 points. Fifty paired repetitions retain the full 3×3 information matrix for scoring.
experiments.explanation: Both methods already have true D-efficiency close to one. The primary-score difference is within tolerance, giving a tie. The new strategy costs more computation without achieving the prespecified endpoint-score improvement. Although parameter fitting is one-dimensional, scoring uses a three-dimensional information determinant. It is not D-efficiency in the constrained parameter space.

experiments.setup: The same two-factor, four-combination binomial model is used, fixing the second main coefficient to zero and estimating the other two under shared constraints. Balanced initialization at 100 points is extended to 1,200, with 50 paired repetitions. Fitting checks both permitted sign branches.
experiments.explanation: The baseline wins, but the paired interval crosses zero. Our method has slightly higher true D-efficiency but a larger deviation of the estimated determinant from its true value, illustrating that design efficiency and the primary score are different objectives. Scoring remains the determinant deviation of the full 3×3 information matrix and cannot be interchanged with auxiliary true D-efficiency.

general estimation improvement. The score is 1-|det(estimated M)/det(optimal I)-1|, without a determinant root or clipping, averaged over repetitions.

Experiment 2: Our method wins and true D-efficiency improves, but parameter error does not decrease. This supports the information-allocation objective, not gains for every estimation target. The original absolute-deviation score based on the estimated information determinant is retained and averaged arithmetically over repetitions.

Experiment 3: Both methods already have true D-efficiency close to one. The primary-score difference is within tolerance, giving a tie. The new strategy costs more computation without achieving the prespecified endpoint-score improvement. Although parameter fitting is one-dimensional, scoring uses a three-dimensional information determinant. It is not D-efficiency in the constrained parameter space.

Experiment 4: The baseline wins, but the paired interval crosses zero. Our method has slightly higher true D-efficiency but a larger deviation of the estimated determinant from its true value, illustrating that design efficiency and the primary score are different objectives. Scoring remains the determinant deviation of the full 3×3 information matrix and cannot be interchanged with auxiliary true D-efficiency.
results_interpretation: The four experiments give one win, one loss and two ties. Expanded closed-form support and uncertainty weighting help for the unknown change point, but do not uniformly improve endpoint scores or parameter error, and increase computation time. Interpretation must distinguish this paper's special relative-information score from conventional D-efficiency.
theory: The selected candidate's one-step weighted logdet gain is at least the expected gain from randomized PICS under the same parameter set. This finite comparison does not establish optimality of the full adaptive trajectory. The original consistency proof requires additional assumptions, and smoothness with an unknown change point needs a separate argument.
limitations: The original metric is not conventional D-efficiency and can rank methods differently from efficiency at the true parameters. Journal-version equivalence, global optimality of nonlinear fitting and the relevant asymptotic conditions are not fully established.

papers.title: A Subsampling Strategy for AIC-based Model Averaging with Generalized Linear Models
papers.short_title: Joint importance sampling for model-averaged coefficients
papers.authors: Jun Yu; HaiYing Wang; Mingyao Ai
papers.research_question: Large-scale generalized linear models may require averaging over multiple candidate models, but repeated full-data fitting is expensive. This paper studies two-stage subsampling to approximate AIC model averaging, asking whether sampling that targets both likelihood and coefficient influence improves finite-subsample coefficient error.
original_method: Original MASS first draws a uniform pilot sample, fits the full model and calculates each observation's likelihood contribution to construct second-stage importance probabilities. A uniform component prevents excessively small sampling probabilities. The two-stage samples are then combined for analysis.

Candidate models are fitted by inverse-probability-weighted likelihood, and AIC with a sampling correction determines model-averaging weights. The original theory mainly controls likelihood-estimation uncertainty. Candidate models may be prespecified or generated by the same forward-selection rule.
our_method: We retain final weighted fitting, candidate-model rules and AIC averaging, changing only second-stage sampling probabilities. Candidate models are first selected on the pilot. Their coefficient-influence norms in the original coordinates and the full model's absolute likelihood contributions are normalized separately and combined into a joint score.

The score uses an equally weighted quadratic combination and retains a 20% uniform mixture. This fixed combination is used in every task to balance coefficient estimation and the original likelihood target. It still requires scoring the full population, but receives neither true coefficients nor full-data reference answers.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline reconstructs weighted likelihood, sandwich AIC and MASS probabilities from the author manuscript, using its six nonzero coefficients, model counts and historical PM2.5 window. Scripts conflicting with the main text were not copied, and the original figures' median-log aggregation is not used.

Each repetition averages original-coordinate L1 error over four sample sizes, including the intercept and padding omitted coefficients with zeros.

Experiment 3: The coefficient-error difference is within the tie range. Small changes in auxiliary classification accuracy do not change this finding; the joint score does not improve approximation of full-data coefficients by the prespecified amount. Experiment 4: Our method wins with a positive paired interval, supporting improved statistical accuracy under this fixed population. results_interpretation: The four experiments give three wins and one tie. Joint probabilities improve coefficient error in three synthetic populations, but do not reach the improvement threshold for real PM2.5 data. Scoring and fitting take longer, so the gain is statistical accuracy at the same subsample size, not execution speed.
theory: Conditional on a fixed population and pilot, the joint proxy's second moment has an explicit minimization structure. The 20% defensive mixture gives a lower bound on probabilities and a finite second-moment inflation factor. That factor is not a guarantee for centered variance or final coefficient error. papers.title: Active Learning for a Recursive Non-Additive Emulator for Multi-Fidelity Computer Experiments
papers.short_title: Transfer structure and uncertainty propagation in multifidelity models
papers.authors: Junoh Heo; Chih-Li Sung
papers.research_question: Relationships between simulators of different accuracies can be nonlinear. When low-fidelity output becomes an input to a high-fidelity model, uncertainty in the lower-level prediction must also be propagated. The paper compares a fixed recursive model with transfer structures selected from training data, examining active sampling and static prediction.
original_method: RNA models each higher-level response as a Gaussian-process function of physical inputs and the preceding level's output. Each level has a constant mean and squared-exponential kernel. Nested training designs provide actual lower-level observations at higher-level training points; prediction integrates over unknown lower-level outputs.

Fixed-parameter moments are analytic for two levels. With three levels, intermediate moments must be matched to a Gaussian distribution. Active sampling uses ALMC: first identify a location with high top-level predictive variance, then select fidelity by expected integrated variance reduction divided by nested-call cost.
our_method: We select among generic constant-mean RNA, linear autoregressive, semiparametric and quadratic-transfer models using training PRESS with a complexity correction. With sufficient samples, quadratic-transfer coefficients may depend on inputs. Selection uses neither test responses nor problem names.

Corresponding analytic moments are derived for the selected affine or quadratic mean. Three-level prediction retains intermediate conditional Gaussian components and combines them with 31-point Gauss–Hermite quadrature rather than immediately collapsing to one Gaussian. Sequential tasks retain ALMC, so model changes also change fidelity allocation.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline follows the 54-page preprint and historical RNAmf implementation for constant-mean RNA, recursive moments and ALMC, retaining 1,000 reference points and 100 future-response imputations. Borehole uses the main text's 60/30 sample sizes and fidelity ordering, which differ from some author scripts.

experiments.label: One-dimensional Perdikaris active learning
experiments.setup: Two noise-free levels have 13/8 initial samples and individual-level costs 1/3, giving initial cost 37 and final cost 80. Ten paired repetitions retain nested sampling. Top-level RMSE is computed on 1,000 independent uniform test points per repetition.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins. Every final fit selects input-dependent quadratic transfer, consistent with the true inter-level relation. Sampling allocation also changes, so the gain cannot be assigned entirely to the trend model. Compute the 1,000-point RMSE in each run, then take its arithmetic mean. The 95% interval uses paired bootstrap.

experiments.label: Four-dimensional Park active learning
experiments.setup: The four-dimensional two-level function starts with 40/20 samples, level costs 1/3, initial cost 100 and final cost 130. Ten paired repetitions spend the full allowed budget. Top-level prediction uses 1,000 independent test points per repetition; each added high-level point also incurs a low-level call.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins, with final selection between semiparametric and quadratic transfer. The limited-budget result supports combined structure selection and active sampling, without isolating one component. Arithmetic mean of RMSE on the original scale; paired-bootstrap 95% interval.

experiments.label: Eight-dimensional Borehole static prediction
experiments.setup: The eight-dimensional two-level Borehole model uses shared 60/30 nested designs, without additional sampling. Fidelity order strictly follows the local preprint. One hundred paired random designs are each evaluated on 1,000 independent uniform points for highest-level error.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins. Identical training points and sample sizes mean the difference comes from prediction and training-based model selection, not more calls or better newly acquired points. Arithmetic mean of 100 RMSEs, with the 60/30 sample sizes and preprint hierarchy held fixed.

experiments.label: Three-level recursive Franke prediction
experiments.setup: A two-dimensional, three-level nonlinear Franke relation uses shared 20/15/10 nested samples without further sampling. One hundred paired random designs are scored on their own independent 1,000-point test sets at level three, jointly testing structure selection and non-Gaussian intermediate propagation.
experiments.explanation: Mean error decreases slightly but not by 5%, giving a tie. Retaining more intermediate-distribution information does not yield a qualifying prediction advantage in this finite-sample task. Arithmetic mean RMSE. Improvement must exceed the prespecified 5% relative tolerance; the interval alone does not determine the verdict.

papers.title: Optimal Designs for Order-of-Addition Two-Level Factorial Experiments
papers.short_title: Joint modeling of order-of-addition and two-level factors
papers.authors: Qiang Zhao; Qian Xiao; Abhyuday Mandal; Fasheng Sun
papers.research_question: When responses depend on both operation order and component levels, a design varying only one may miss important structure. The paper studies orthogonal designs covering both, and compares the original extended linear model with richer interaction and position-effect models on fixed training designs.
original_method: The original compound model represents permutations by pairwise order variables and includes component-level main effects. The extended model adds pairwise interactions between component levels. Doubly orthogonal arrays require the appropriate balanced counts for order and levels; strongly doubly orthogonal arrays additionally require fourth-order level orthogonality.

For small designs, binary programming finds feasible arrays and candidate selection uses extended-model D-efficiency. Larger designs fold together order orthogonal arrays and two-level orthogonal arrays. Theoretical optimality concerns the specified model information matrix, not prediction for every possible true response.
our_method: Both modifications retain the designs actually generated by the original method. For four operations, training responses are appropriately shifted and logged. Basic order and level terms remain unpenalized, while added order/level interactions receive a fixed ridge penalty. Predictions are transformed back to the original response scale.

For scheduling, we augment the original extended model by sequence-position-indexed levels and their second-order products, fitted by least squares. They represent position effects caused by squared cumulative processing times. True cost weights are not supplied; coefficients are estimated solely from the shared training responses.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline enforces the original binary count constraints and SDOA foldover construction, then fits extended-model OLS. For four operations, each run selects the highest D-efficiency among 20 feasible candidates, only the best within the budget. The six-job task constructs 192 treatments afresh rather than reusing author-reported scores.

experiments.label: Order and levels of four arithmetic operations
experiments.setup: The full set of 384 treatments combines permutations of four operations and two-level combinations. Each run selects 24 shared training treatments. Ten outer random designs each generate 100 shared initial values and apply addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. Prediction is scored on the remaining 360 treatments, without added response noise.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins through transformation and interaction ridge modeling on an identical design. Without separate ablations, the gains cannot be assigned individually to the log transformation, extra terms or regularization. First average RMSE over the 100 response instances, then over 10 outer seeds; this is not the original paper's median.

experiments.label: Six-job single-machine scheduling
experiments.setup: From all 46,080 order/processing-time combinations, a shared 192-point strongly doubly orthogonal design is used for training. Each outer seed permutes 100 sets of position-cost weights. Response is revenue minus squared cumulative-completion-time cost. Ten outer repetitions evaluate prediction on the remaining 45,888 treatments.
experiments.explanation: The modified error reaches near machine precision. The selected noise-free response lies exactly in the added quadratic-position model space and the training-rank condition holds. This is not zero error for a general black box. Average each seed's 100 RMSEs, then average over 10 seeds. Near-zero values are at floating-point precision.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 2: The modified error reaches near machine precision. The selected noise-free response lies exactly in the added quadratic-position model space and the training-rank condition holds. This is not zero error for a general black box. Average each seed's 100 RMSEs, then average over 10 seeds. Near-zero values are at floating-point precision.
results_interpretation: Both experiments improve prediction, but both methods use the same designs, so the gain is not higher D-efficiency. Four operations demonstrate empirical value of the combined prediction model. Near-zero scheduling error has a structural explanation: missing quadratic-position terms are added, rather than true weights being supplied.
theory: Foldover cancellation, information upper bounds and same-rank exact recovery in the quadratic-position model can be proved. Scheduling training rank is 56 and spans the response space. A 24-run design, however, cannot satisfy fourth-order OA divisibility, and the best finite candidate is not an exactly globally optimal SDOA.
limitations: The exact D2 set in the authors' Example 4 and interpretation of normal-distribution parameters are not fully verified. Exact scheduling recovery is limited to noise-free quadratic-position responses. Other supplementary applications were not run.

papers.short_title: Robust optimization under environmental disturbances with quadratic trends
papers.authors: John J. Miller; Simon Mak
papers.research_question: Robust optimization targets expected response under a distribution of environmental disturbances, while one simulation observes only one control/disturbance combination. The paper studies joint input selection to find the maximizer of expected response with limited simulations, rather than merely fitting the entire response surface.
original_method: Original TVR fits a Gaussian process jointly over control and disturbance variables, then integrates over the known disturbance distribution to obtain a posterior for the target expectation. Selection combines the probability that a candidate control exceeds the current recommendation and the reduction in its expected-response variance from a joint simulation.

After each query, the model is refitted and the joint acquisition function optimized. The final recommendation maximizes the integrated posterior mean and need not be a previously simulated location. This directly targets robustness, unlike finding the largest observed value over controls alone.
our_method: We attempt a full quadratic trend from observed data, using it only if sample-size, rank, condition-number and strict PRESS checks all pass; otherwise the mean remains constant. Known disturbance moments integrate the trend, while residuals retain the original integrated-GP structure.

Joint selection instead uses knowledge gradient on a finite set of control decisions: expected improvement in the best posterior mean after a new observation, analytically integrated through the upper envelope of Gaussian-affine functions. The decision set is finite, but queries are still searched over the common control/disturbance domain. Estimated parameters remain fixed within one acquisition calculation.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline reimplements integrated GP posteriors, TVR and sequential fitting from the 39-page preprint; author software was unavailable. Trid strictly follows the printed formula with both terms negative. Probability normalization and disturbance-parameter interpretations were fixed in advance. Reproduction of journal curves is not claimed.

papers.title: A Construction Method for Maximin L1-Distance Latin Hypercube Designs
papers.short_title: Distance optimization of group-constructed Latin hypercubes
papers.authors: Ru Yuan; Yuhao Yin; Hongquan Xu; Min-Qian Liu
papers.research_question: A Latin hypercube uses every level uniformly in each column, yet its closest pair of rows can still be very close. The paper uses modular arithmetic and group structure to construct large designs, seeking better construction moduli and level labels while retaining dimensions and the Latin property.
original_method: The original algorithm takes representatives coprime to modulus N and no greater than N/2. A square matrix is formed from the smaller of each modular product and its negative, and representatives are then replaced consistently by their ranked level labels. The result is both a Latin square and a Latin hypercube.

Some doubly even moduli additionally give mirror-complement relations, allowing the first half of the columns to form a rectangular design. Efficiency is minimum L1 row distance divided by the mean-distance upper bound. The paper proves equidistant optimality for some prime moduli and studies other families numerically.
our_method: We retain the specified original design as a candidate, search other bounded moduli producing the same number of rows, and first select a better-distance algebraic construction. Global level labels are then exchanged on the group table using exact distance increments. The retained result is no worse than the original design.

For half-column designs, label search preserves mirror complementarity and the original distance relations. Group structure reduces redundant square-design distance calculations. These operations optimize construction parameters and labels without changing dimensions, level sets or the primary denominator, and do not claim exhaustive search of all designs.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline directly implements the journal's Algorithm 1 with each scenario's specified N and original label order, retaining the original first half of columns where required. Our method may select an alternative same-size auxiliary modulus, so the baseline is not the best design over every modulus allowed by the original paper.

experiments.label: Half-column designs from doubly even moduli
experiments.setup: For all 44 primes p from 5 to 199, N=4p gives n=p-1 and s=n/2, up to 198×99. Each method completes the panel 5 times, retaining integer Latin levels. Auxiliary L2 metrics use the same final designs.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins through mirror-preserving label search. It improves 37/44 scenarios, but the worst-scenario efficiency is unchanged; not every size improves strictly. Average equally over 44 scenarios, then over 5 repetitions. The denominator remains the original mean-distance upper bound.

experiments.label: Doubly even composite-modulus squares
experiments.setup: For 40 primes from 16 to 200, both N=8p and N=16p are run, giving 80 squares up to 792×792. Each of 5 paired repetitions covers every scenario. Methods construct and score independently under a common computation cap.
experiments.explanation: Every scenario improves and the panel is a win. Traces show that auxiliary-modulus selection supplies most of the initial gain, partly using constructions already proved optimal in the paper. These optimal families are not newly proved here. Give the two construction families equal weight, average equally over primes within each family, then over 5 repetitions. The reference upper bound is unchanged.

experiments.label: Odd composite-modulus squares
experiments.setup: For all 40 primes from 13 to 200, moduli 5p, 7p, 11p and 13p give 160 scenarios, up to 1188×1188. Each of 5 paired seeds completes all four families, comparing minimum-L1-distance efficiency of same-size designs.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins. Most, but not all, scenarios improve strictly. Modulus choice supplies the main gain and subsequent label search adds more; this sequential decomposition is not an independent ablation. Give four families equal weight and their 40 primes equal weight, then average over seeds.

experiments.label: Prime-square and prime-cube constructions
experiments.setup: The square family uses 23 primes from 5 to 100; the cube family uses p=5,7,11,13,17,19, giving 29 scenarios up to 4656×4656. Each method completes 5 repetitions. The size cap covers only the prespecified portion of the original cube curves.
experiments.explanation: The panel wins, but only 7/29 scenarios improve and all five primary scores are identical. The largest design does not improve. The result supports this fixed panel, not general improvement frequencies or random-variation behavior. Square and cube families each receive half the weight, averaging within 23 and 6 scenarios respectively. This is not a direct average of 29 scenarios.

Experiment 4: The panel wins, but only 7/29 scenarios improve and all five primary scores are identical. The largest design does not improve. results_interpretation: All four panels improve mean L1 efficiency, but gains are small and not universal across scenarios. theory: Group-relative distances, mirror preservation and O(n) exchange increments admit exact derivations. Retaining the baseline ensures non-deterioration in successful runs. limitations: Specified-N baselines and same-size modulus searches cover different spaces; this is not a claim to beat the best construction among all original candidates. Some general asymptotic-optimality claims lack complete proofs; a finite panel is not an asymptotic argument.

papers.title: Minimum Aberration Factorial Designs Under a Mixed Parametrization
papers.short_title: Exact search for factorial designs with mixed parameterizations
papers.authors: Guanzhou Chen; Boxin Tang
papers.research_question: Some factors have default levels to protect, whereas others use symmetric effect coding. Standard aberration ordering does not apply directly to their mixture. The paper defines criteria through contamination of main-effect estimates by higher-order interactions, comparing local-neighborhood search with complete search within fixed orthogonal templates.
original_method: The original method codes default-level B factors as 0 and 2 and other O factors as -1 and 1, and computes contamination matrices from omitted interactions to each type of main effect. With B effects prioritized, the two contaminations are compared alternately; with equal importance, total contamination is compared. Both use lexicographic ordering by interaction order.

The paper provides both complete catalog enumeration and local search starting from low-aberration orthogonal arrays. Local search sequentially uses cross-group single- and double-column swaps and single- and double-sign flips of B columns, accepting only strict improvement to find good mixed-coded designs at lower cost.
our_method: Within the same three 20×13 templates as the baseline, we enumerate every B-column subset and sign assignment. Because the first two contamination components are invariant to sign flips, a strictly worse prefix safely eliminates all signs for that subset. Tied prefixes proceed through all later components.

A row-pair generating polynomial evaluates exact integer contamination numerators, avoiding construction of every interaction matrix for each candidate. Both arms share this scorer, so the main comparison is local stopping versus complete within-domain search. Enumeration already present in the original paper is not claimed as new.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline implements the four neighborhoods and specified cycling order of Section 4.2 of the accepted manuscript, using three public GMA templates and shared initial states. The public author repository contains result files but no runnable algorithm source; this is an independent implementation from the text.

experiments.label: Priority for default-level factors
experiments.setup: Twenty runs, 13 factors and three GMA orthogonal templates cover all B-factor counts from 1 to 13. Forty paired random initial states are used. Each run selects the full lexicographic best among three templates, first requiring both second-order contaminations to attain their prescribed within-domain minima.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins without sacrificing preceding contamination components. Complete search reduces third-order contamination left by local stopping, but the domain remains the three fixed templates. Average πB3 equally over the 13 B-factor counts, then over 40 repetitions. This is a contamination norm, not response MSE.

experiments.label: Equal importance for all main effects
experiments.setup: The same three 20×13 templates cover B-factor counts 1–13, with shared random starts for each template and 40 paired repetitions. Search uses the full lexicographic total-contamination vector, requiring the corresponding minimum second-order total contamination before comparing the primary third-order component.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins, with the same within-domain optimum in every repetition. Zero standard deviation reflects deterministic complete search, not absence of uncertainty for every orthogonal array or other size. Each run averages π3 equally over 13 settings. It chooses the best template rather than averaging the three templates.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 1: Our method wins without sacrificing preceding contamination components. Complete search reduces third-order contamination left by local stopping, but the domain remains the three fixed templates. Average πB3 equally over the 13 B-factor counts, then over 40 repetitions. This is a contamination norm, not response MSE.

Experiment 2: Our method wins, with the same within-domain optimum in every repetition. Zero standard deviation reflects deterministic complete search, not absence of uncertainty for every orthogonal array or other size. Each run averages π3 equally over 13 settings. It chooses the best template rather than averaging the three templates.
results_interpretation: Both experiments yield small, checkable contamination reductions, supporting exact search at this finite template size. It takes longer but meets the common budget. The result does not exceed the global optimum from the original full enumeration and cannot extend fixed-template optimality to all 730 isomorphism classes.
theory: Regression-operator simplification, row-pair scoring and strict-prefix pruning can be proved step by step. On completion, full search certifies the lexicographic optimum of the entire contamination vector within the three templates. It covers neither unenumerated templates nor all nonorthogonal designs.
limitations: Only three GMA templates are used; the full catalog of 730 classes and catalogs with more factors were not run. Forty repetitions are fewer than the original 200. Equivalence between the accepted manuscript and final journal layout is unconfirmed.
