papers.title: QuIP: Experimental Design for Expensive Simulators with Many Qualitative Factors via Integer Programming
papers.short_title: Combinatorial design and active learning with high-dimensional qualitative inputs
papers.authors: Yen-Chun Liu; Simon Mak
papers.research_question: Continuous distances and gradients do not directly apply when many inputs are unordered categories. QuIP expresses qualitative design as integer programming and uses an exchangeable-kernel GP for prediction and optimization. This comparison contrasts time-limited exact formulations with balanced construction, regularized modeling and categorical-neighborhood search.
original_method: The original method chooses initial designs by minimum Hamming distance, using one-hot encoding and feasibility programs with progressively increased target distance to allocate categorical levels. Surrogate correlation depends on whether each input agrees, allowing different categorical factors to have different learned influence scales.

Prediction maximizes posterior variance; optimization uses UCB, combining mean and standard deviation. Acquisition is formulated as integer programming over the entire categorical domain, with model refitting at each step. Formulation equivalence establishes matching objectives, not globally optimal solutions within finite time limits.
our_method: Initial design instead uses balanced-column exchange search, with edge-disjoint pair constructions controlling row overlaps where applicable. Reaching an independent counting upper bound provides an optimality certificate. The resulting designs are still evaluated by their actual minimum Hamming distance.

Sequential tasks add fixed log-scale regularization and select candidates by multistart categorical-neighborhood search. Maze prediction retains maximum variance; snake optimization switches to expected improvement. An analytic integrated-variance candidate was derived but not used in the final comparison.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline implements integer objectives from the 40-page preprint, replacing Gurobi with CP-SAT and SCIP and correcting the initial ball bound and UCB sign. Each fitting/search step has only 4 seconds; most integer programs stop at the limit. Results therefore compare feasible solutions under this budget.

experiments.label: Nine qualitative initial-design settings
experiments.setup: Every design has 50 rows. Each of 10, 20 and 30 category levels is paired with three dimensions, giving nine settings from 15 to 55 dimensions. Each setting has 40 seconds of construction time, with 8 paired repetitions per method and all minimum Hamming distances included.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins. Of 72 formal designs, 64 attain the common counting bound, versus 8 for the baseline. Certification does not cover every instance, and a time-limited unsolved instance is not infeasible. Divide minimum distance by dimension within a setting, then average equally across nine settings and 8 repetitions.

experiments.label: Prediction of twelve-step maze paths
experiments.setup: A 6×6 maze has five actions per step and twelve steps, giving 5¹² paths. Forty shared initial paths are extended to 200 training paths, with 4 seconds per step and 8 paired repetitions. Final endpoint-cost predictions are evaluated on 5,000 independent test paths.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins. Regularization and categorical-neighborhood search both change while sampling remains maximum variance. The evidence supports the combination, not separate contributions. The RRMSE denominator uses the sum of squared test-response deviations from the test mean, not training variance or response mean square.

experiments.label: Reward optimization for twelve-step snake paths
experiments.setup: An 8×8 map has 17 prize cells, twelve steps and five actions per step. Forty shared initial paths are extended to 200 distinct paths. Fitting and selection receive 4 seconds per step, with 8 paired repetitions. Scoring uses the highest cumulative reward among actually queried paths.
experiments.explanation: Mean reward meets the win criterion, but only 5/8 pairs improve and the interval crosses zero. Regularization, expected improvement and neighborhood search change jointly, so this is not a stable single-component advantage. Average raw rewards under fixed prizes and common simulation rules that allow a path to return after moving outside the map.

limitations: Later author snake code differs in two prize locations, prize consumption and out-of-bounds handling, so this is not a journal reproduction. Most baseline acquisitions lack global-solution certificates under the strict per-step limit. Rover and other applications were not run.

papers.title: A Hierarchical Expected Improvement Method for Bayesian Optimization
papers.short_title: Local and global exploration in hierarchical expected improvement
papers.authors: Zhehui Chen; Simon Mak; C. F. Jeff Wu
papers.research_question: Ordinary expected improvement can stop exploring too early when surrogate variance is underestimated. The paper uses a hierarchical GP to improve exploration. This study asks whether adaptive local search and periodic uniform queries further reduce final regret of noise-free black-box functions at equal call counts.
original_method: Original HEI gives hierarchical priors to the mean and process scale, yielding a Student-t predictive distribution for expected improvement. The selected HEI-DSD variant grows its scale prior with sample size to avoid premature collapse of uncertainty.

Initial data select a polynomial trend by BIC and estimate hyperparameters; correlation scales and the globally searched HEI optimum are subsequently updated. Numerical fitting and acquisition optimization are still required. A local optimizer's success status does not establish the theory's exact-maximization assumption.
our_method: We retain the global hierarchical model and HEI formula, but search mainly in a rectangle around the current best point. Its directional widths follow learned length scales, expanding after consecutive successes and shrinking after consecutive failures, with periodic returns to global search.

One global uniform query is scheduled per ten sequential calls to retain exploration independently of surrogate correctness. These queries count normally against the budget. The combination draws on local Bayesian optimization but is not a complete TuRBO implementation.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline implements HEI-DSD, Student-t acquisition and trend variance from the 42-page preprint, following the text for differences such as the author code's BIC coefficient. Both arms share initialization and finite multistart solving. Some fits do not report success but retain finite best candidates under the shared rule.

experiments.label: Two-dimensional Six-Hump Camel
experiments.setup: The noise-free Camel function is minimized on [-2,2]². A shared 20-point approximate maximin Latin initialization is followed by 100 calls, totaling 120. Twenty paired repetitions are scored by the minimum among all observed values minus the known global minimum.
experiments.explanation: Both errors are already very small; absolute improvement is far below tolerance, giving a tie. The roughly 86% relative change arises from a tiny denominator and is not a practically large victory. Arithmetic mean of original-scale regret. The auxiliary log-transformed metric measures a different statistic.

experiments.label: Six-dimensional Levy
experiments.setup: Levy is minimized on [-10,10]6 with 60 shared initial points and 60 additional calls, totaling 120, over 20 paired repetitions. The primary score includes initial and subsequent observations and retains poor but complete valid runs.
experiments.explanation: The baseline wins. A few large failures substantially increase our method's mean. The interval still crosses zero, distinguishing the prespecified mean-based verdict from statistical confirmation of population superiority. Arithmetic mean of all 20 endpoint regrets, including a few large valid values.

experiments.label: Ten-dimensional Ackley
experiments.setup: Ackley is optimized on [-5,5]¹0. After 100 shared initial points only 20 additional calls remain, with 10 paired repetitions and 120 total calls. Our 20 steps comprise 5 global HEI, 13 local HEI and 2 uniform queries.
experiments.explanation: The baseline wins. Little budget remains after initialization, so allocation changes may matter, but no ablation attributes deterioration specifically to local regions or uniform queries. Local search and safeguard exploration have theoretical motivation but do not improve results at these finite budgets. papers.title: Tuning differential evolution algorithm for constructing uniform projection designs
papers.short_title: Exact exchange search for uniform-projection designs
papers.authors: Samuel Onyambu; Hongquan Xu
papers.research_question: Latin hypercubes ensure marginal uniformity but not uniform two-dimensional projections. The paper studies lower mean two-dimensional discrepancy at equal candidate-evaluation counts, comparing the original tuned differential-evolution scheme with iterated exchange search concentrating the available budget.
original_method: The original differential-evolution population consists of whole design matrices. Mutation swaps two row positions within columns; crossover combines mutant and target columns; only improving candidates are accepted. Every column retains all discrete levels, preserving the Latin constraint. The objective is mean squared centered discrepancy over all two-dimensional projections.

DEoptim first tries 11 mutation probabilities, each with 100 individuals for 100 generations, with complementary crossover probabilities. After choosing the best parameter, it starts a fresh 100-individual population for 1,500 generations. The presearch design is not used directly as the final output.
our_method: We keep the best of 100 shared initial designs, mix adjacent-level exchanges with arbitrary-row exchanges, and after sustained stagnation perturb the historical best before resuming strict descent. Every proposal, rejected exchange and perturbation counts toward the candidate-evaluation budget.

Existing distance identities convert discrepancy ordering to an integer-objective comparison and yield a single-exchange increment formula. Scoring and updating the distance state take time linear in the number of rows. This accelerates established iterated local search; it is not claimed as a new global optimizer.
papers.baseline_implementation: DEoptim is reimplemented from the 39-page author working paper and code, correcting initialization, random-number handling and related issues. Both methods evaluate 261,200 candidates per run and share the final initial population. Each experiment has 20 paired repetitions rather than the original 100; journal-version equivalence is unverified.

experiments.label: 30-row, 3-column design
experiments.setup: Construct a 30×3 discrete Latin hypercube with each column a permutation of 0–29. Both arms share 100 initial designs and a cap of 261,200 candidate evaluations including tuning and search. Twenty paired repetitions score the final design's three two-dimensional projections.
experiments.explanation: Improvement exceeds the prespecified threshold and the paired interval is positive. Concentrated budget use and retention of the historical best are plausible explanations, without ablations isolating each step. Arithmetic mean of 20 final metrics; no square root is taken, and this is not full-dimensional discrepancy.

experiments.label: 50-row, 5-column design
experiments.setup: Construct a 50×5 discrete Latin hypercube with levels 0–49 in each column. Ten two-dimensional projections enter equally. The shared population, 261,200-evaluation cap and 20 paired repetitions are retained, with every final design saved.
experiments.explanation: The mean decreases slightly but not beyond the tie threshold, and the interval crosses zero. The auxiliary worst-projection metric worsens slightly, so improvement of an average does not mean improvement of every projection. Average the ten projections within a run, then average over 20 repetitions.

experiments.label: 70-row, 7-column design
experiments.setup: Construct a 70×7 discrete Latin hypercube with levels 0–69 and 21 two-dimensional projections. Both methods share initialization, a 261,200-candidate cap and 20 paired repetitions. Other original competing searches and prediction experiments are excluded.
experiments.explanation: Improvement exceeds the threshold with a positive interval, and this implementation is faster. papers.title: Fixed-budget optimal designs for multi-fidelity computer experiments
papers.short_title: Multifidelity nested-design optimization under fixed cost
papers.authors: Gecheng Chen; Rui Tuo
papers.research_question: Multifidelity simulation requires both sample allocation across levels and spatial point selection. The paper predicts the highest finite-fidelity response at fixed simulation cost, comparing allocation driven by an asymptotic error bound with direct optimization of predictive risk on finite reference points, across dimensions and misspecified design parameters.
original_method: The original model writes each response level as a sum of independent Matérn GP increments whose variances decay geometrically. Under nesting, differences of paid observations at adjacent levels can be interpolated separately and summed. The target is the highest finite level, not an infinite-accuracy limit.

An error upper bound and level costs yield continuous sample proportions, followed by rounding and greedy use of the remaining budget to obtain nested sample counts. Locations are Halton prefixes. The strategy primarily optimizes counts; posterior variance at actual finite locations does not enter the original allocation formula directly.
our_method: We evaluate predictive variance at 1,024 independent fixed reference points and construct an ALC sequence from 512 candidate locations. Integer dynamic programming allocates samples over Halton and ALC prefixes separately under cost and nesting constraints. The original baseline is explicitly retained as a candidate.

The minimum-reference-risk choice among allocation, location and combined modifications receives one round of nested coordinate exchange. A location moves simultaneously in every level containing it, preserving nesting and budget. Response generation and the fixed-kernel predictor remain shared; additional computation is concentrated in design.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline is reconstructed from the main text of the 33-page preprint without verifiable author code. Main-text and appendix exponents and some tabulated sample counts disagree; the main-text formulas are used. Base variance, length scale and test sampling are prespecified. Misspecification affects design only; prediction retains the true kernel.

experiments.setup: A four-level GP on [0,15] has variance decay 1/3, Matérn smoothness 1.25, level costs 1,8,64,512 and total budget 4,760. Thirty paired repetitions each use 200 shared independent test points to assess highest-level prediction.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins, changing sample counts from (96,39,20,6) to (144,57,25,5). Allocation and locations change together, so their separate contributions are not identified. Compute test RMSE within a repetition, then average arithmetically over 30 repetitions.

papers.title: Stacking Designs: Designing Multifidelity Computer Experiments with Target Predictive Accuracy
papers.short_title: Multifidelity extrapolation and kernel interpolation at target accuracy
papers.authors: Chih-Li Sung; Yi (Irene) Ji; Simon Mak; Wenjia Wang; Tao Tang
papers.research_question: Multifidelity responses contain both discretization and surrogate-interpolation error. Within the simulation budget actually consumed by the original stacking design, this study asks whether learning error decay from paid multilevel responses and directly extrapolating improves prediction of the infinite-accuracy response, while separating empirical target attainment from rigorous certification.
original_method: Original stacking builds a Matérn-kernel interpolant for each difference between adjacent response levels and sums the interpolants. Kernel power functions and estimated function norms quantify surrogate error. Simulation costs determine nested sample counts, and fidelity levels are added progressively.

Richardson-type decay estimates numerical bias, and each error component is compared with half the target tolerance. Function norms and decay order are estimated from training data, so the practical stopping rule is not itself continuous-domain certification. The original asymptotic theorem also needs additional regularity and mesh assumptions.
our_method: From adjacent differences at three paid initial levels, we estimate a common contraction rate q by least squares. If numerical-identifiability, interval and residual checks pass, adjacent responses are combined for Richardson extrapolation and the combined response is fitted directly, avoiding separate interpolation of large canceling components.

Remaining paired budget goes to finite candidates with the largest kernel power function, charging all required lower-level calls. Kernel parameters are refitted every eight samples. Unstable estimates trigger higher-level pairing; q outside the allowed interval triggers fallback to finite-fidelity response. Geometric errors therefore do not automatically yield exact debiasing.
papers.baseline_implementation: The original stacking method is reconstructed from the 32-page preprint and author code, following the text's raw-response and error definitions. Both Poisson methods share an open P1 finite-element solver and response integration, replacing MATLAB meshing and the code's nodal mean. Identical original stopping trajectories are not expected.

experiments.label: Two-dimensional Currin extrapolation
experiments.setup: The Currin response on the unit square has exact geometric level bias. Six levels cost 4–4096 per call, with 10 initial points per level, a 200-point per-level cap and target L2 error 1. Ten paired repetitions use 8,192 independent Sobol test points. Our method cannot exceed the paired baseline's cost.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins substantially, consistent with the exact geometric bias structure. Simulation cost is lower but total method time slightly longer. Passing the test target does not certify the original internal error estimate. Mean of 10 finite-test L2 errors; paired-bootstrap 95% interval.

experiments.label: Integrated Poisson response
experiments.setup: The integral of a zero-boundary Poisson solution is predicted over physical inputs [-1,1]. Six P1 mesh spacings range from 0.2 to 0.00625, with target maximum error 0.05. Ten paired repetitions use 2,001 shared test-grid points, with costs based on newly measured levelwise FEM costs.
experiments.metric: Maximum absolute error on the test grid
experiments.explanation: Our method wins, but both arms use only five initial points at each of the first three levels, at identical cost, without additional greedy sampling. The gain comes from extrapolation and surrogate construction on the same paid initial data. Mean of 10 grid-maximum errors; paired-bootstrap 95% interval. The continuous-domain supremum is not certified.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use paired bootstrap.

Experiment 2: Our method wins, but both arms use only five initial points at each of the first three levels, at identical cost, without additional greedy sampling. The gain comes from extrapolation and surrogate construction on the same paid initial data. Mean of 10 grid-maximum errors; paired-bootstrap 95% interval. The continuous-domain supremum is not certified.
results_interpretation: Both experiments win, supporting exploitation of correlated multilevel error for finite-budget prediction. Empirical target attainment is 9/10 versus 10/10 for Currin and 10/10 for both Poisson methods. Internal stopping states differ, so these empirical success rates cannot be called theoretical certification rates.
theory: The extrapolation perturbation decomposition and regularized RKHS error bound hold conditionally. However, the implementation claim that geometric levels ensure exact debiasing omits numerical identifiability and 0.05≤q≤0.9. An estimate q=0.95 causes fallback and no exact debiasing. limitations: The original preprint's complexity proof has gaps including constant dependence; no replacement asymptotic proof is provided. The turbine-blade application was not run. Equivalence of the open FEM solver and the authors' MATLAB meshes is unproved.

papers.title: Fast Approximation of Shapley Values Through Fractional Factorial Designs
papers.short_title: Shapley estimation with fractional factorial designs and stratified control variates
papers.authors: Zheng Zhou; Robert Mee; Herbert Hamers; Wei Zheng
papers.research_question: Shapley values average marginal contributions over many participant coalitions, making exact enumeration rapidly impractical as participant count grows. This study asks whether fractional factorial designs can reduce coalition queries, with a small correction for high-order interactions, to improve allocation accuracy at equal query budgets.
original_method: The original method encodes coalition membership as two-level factors, builds a fractional factorial design from recursive Hadamard structure, and combines responses according to aliasing relations to obtain preliminary Shapley values. These linear combinations are exact under a truncation condition on higher-order interactions.

For games such as voting and airport cost sharing that violate truncation, preliminary contributions identify key participants. Latin-square sampling supplies calibration values, and a test selects proportional normalization or smoothing-spline correction. The market example uses only the recursive design.
our_method: We use complementary sampling stratified by coalition size, with one query informing several participants. A pilot estimates linear control variates and residual sizes within strata. Coefficients and allocations are then fixed, and an independent main sample estimates residuals with known control expectations added back.

Some boundary coalition-size strata are evaluated exactly, and every output's total contribution equals the grand-coalition value. Our budget is only the actual query count of the paired baseline. Evaluation-reference formulas are not supplied, and the baseline's fitted spline is not treated as the true contribution function.
papers.baseline_implementation: Algorithms 1 and 2 are independently implemented; splines call R's npreg. Where the author script's regression direction conflicts with the text, the text is used. Fixed voting and airport instances are regenerated at the original sizes, without promising the authors' original random-number outcomes.

experiments.label: Weighted voting with 129 participants
experiments.setup: A fixed game has 129 distinct integer weights and a threshold of half the total weight. One hundred paired random repetitions match each baseline's actual coalition-query budget. An independent integer dynamic program computes exact reference Shapley values.
experiments.explanation: Error decreases substantially and our method wins, supporting complementary stratification and residual correction in this high-order voting game. Component contributions have not been separated by ablations. Sum squared errors over all participants, then average over 100 runs, without division by participant count.

experiments.label: Airport cost sharing with 257 participants
experiments.setup: A fixed instance has 257 ascending airport-requirement weights, allowing duplicates; coalition cost is their maximum. One hundred paired repetitions limit our queries to the paired baseline's count. An independent analytic formula provides the error reference.
experiments.explanation: Our method reduces error without additional coalition queries, supporting direct residual estimation for this airport instance. It does not establish superiority over spline correction for every airport game. Mean of 100 total squared errors. Every baseline run enters spline correction under the original test.

experiments.label: Market value for 17 firms
experiments.setup: The full public 17×17 market matrix is retained; coalition values include own revenue and external effects. One hundred paired repetitions use references cross-checked by all 2^17 coalitions and a quadratic formula. Budgets come from paired recursive designs.
experiments.explanation: Both methods reach floating-point rounding scale and tie. The value function is quadratic, and both methods have applicable exactness arguments. Auxiliary query differences do not alter the verdict. Both errors are about 10-²7. Relative percentages are sensitive to rounding and should be interpreted through absolute error and the tie verdict.

papers.title: Group Sequential Design with Posterior and Posterior Predictive Probabilities
papers.short_title: Two-anchor probability interpolation for Bayesian sequential trial design
papers.authors: Luke Hagar; Shirin Golchi; Marina B. Klein
papers.research_question: Three-stage binary clinical trials jointly select sample size, success thresholds and futility thresholds. Nested simulation at every sample size is costly. The paper approximates complete stopping probabilities from a few anchors and asks how to approach prescribed error-spending and power targets more accurately while borrowing historical information.
original_method: The original method generates full null and alternative trial paths at two sample-size anchors and computes posterior success and posterior predictive probabilities. Marginal order statistics are logit-transformed and interpolated linearly in sample size. Rankings from one anchor reconstruct dependence across stages.

For each candidate sample size, success thresholds are calibrated first, followed by futility thresholds. The smallest integer size with estimated power at least 0.85 is selected. Predictive-design scenarios bin generating effects to retain effect heterogeneity.
our_method: We interpolate margins on the probit and square-root-sample-size scales and combine both anchors' empirical dependence structures, restoring the appropriate joint samples at both endpoints. The success/failure threshold-search grid is refined from 10-4 to 10-6.

Both methods share Beta-mixture prior updating and finite-sum predictive probabilities in place of original nested sampling; this shared correction is not credited solely to our method. After a final design is submitted, independent confirmation paths estimate actual stopping frequencies rather than using interpolation predictions as test results.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline is reconstructed from the 23-page arXiv working paper and author code. Shared corrections address mixture-sampling weight indices, the D2 null and success-priority stopping. Both use an exact finite-sum engine, so this is not a point-for-point reproduction of the authors' nested Monte Carlo program.

experiments.setup: The three-stage trial uses control probability 0.7, null treatment probability 0.7 and alternative 0.8. experiments.explanation: Calibration error decreases and our method wins, mainly through second-stage futility and final power closer to target. Not every error-probability component improves. experiments.setup: Control probability is 0.75, null treatment probability 0.75 and alternative 0.843; other three-stage priors and spending targets are unchanged. Few repetitions and random-effect mixing limit extrapolation of exact-interpolation results. Despite a substantial relative reduction in the mean, absolute improvement does not exceed 0.002. papers.title: Modeling and Active Learning for Experiments with Quantitative-Sequence Factors
papers.short_title: Joint quantity–permutation Gaussian processes and active learning
papers.authors: Qian Xiao; Yaping Wang; Abhyuday Mandal; Xinwei Deng
papers.research_question: Some responses depend jointly on component quantities and application order, so neither a continuous-only nor a permutation-only model suffices. This study evaluates whether a joint surrogate finds better quantity–order combinations within limited queries and predicts unobserved combinations accurately.
original_method: Original MaGP expresses the response as a sum of component GPs. Each component depends on its quantity difference and latent-position distance. Components share a two-dimensional position mapping; likelihood estimates quantity scales, variances and position coordinates, followed by predictive means and expected improvement.

Original QS learning alternates continuous-quantity optimization and permutation search: genetic and local search for quantities, and space-filling threshold accepting for permutations. Each response triggers refitting, with stopping by expected improvement or the query cap.
our_method: We use a position/Mallows interaction kernel to represent component quantity and position, differences between whole permutations, and joint quantity interactions. Responses are standardized from training data. Log-parameterized covariances, weak penalties and multiple starts aim to stabilize finite-sample fitting.

Active search uses multistart continuous expected-improvement optimization with complete swap and insertion neighborhoods; drug candidates are fully enumerated. Both optimization tasks spend the full allowed budget instead of stopping after consecutive small expected improvements. Kernel, fitting and search change together and are interpreted as a complete procedure.
papers.baseline_implementation: MaGP and QS-EGO are independently implemented from the author manuscript and R code, retaining original prediction-task scaling, parameter ranges and fitting budgets. Traveling-salesman position encoding and quantity accumulation are corrected from the text and shared by both methods; profits are not directly comparable with the authors' original values.

experiments.label: Eight-city quantity–order traveling salesman
experiments.setup: A fixed eight-city route problem, deadlines and the authors' 46-point initial design are used. City service quantities range from 1 to 4, with a cap of 88 evaluations. Five paired searches use the same simulator and compare the highest actually queried profit.
experiments.explanation: Our mean profit is lower, so the original method wins. The instance does not support the new kernel/search combination, and the aggregate result cannot identify which component caused the decrease. Arithmetic mean of the five best profits, not a surrogate maximum or author-reported profit.

experiments.label: Replay of 24 lymphoma treatments
experiments.setup: All 24 dose/order combinations of three drugs from the public table are used, with eight fixed initial treatments and at most 15 queries. Only queried responses may be read. Twenty paired optimization repetitions neither recollect nor perturb biological data.
experiments.explanation: Our method has higher mean inhibition and finds the table's best treatment in every repetition, but uses one more query on average. The gain is not attributable solely to the kernel and is not clinical efficacy evidence. Mean best inhibition rate over 20 repetitions; increments are percentage points. Repetition reflects optimization randomness, not biological replication.

experiments.label: Quantity–order prediction for four operations
experiments.setup: Each repetition generates 31 training inputs and 2,400 independent test inputs, with 100 occurrences of each of 24 operation permutations in testing. Responses sequentially apply addition, subtraction, multiplication and division without observation noise. One hundred paired repetitions share training/test splits.
experiments.explanation: Our method substantially reduces prediction error under this simulation distribution. Interaction kernels, standardization, regularization and multiple starts change together; their independent effects are not separated. Compute RMSE over each repetition's 2,400 test points, then average over 100 repetitions.

papers.title: Adaptive design for Gaussian process regression under censoring
papers.short_title: Input warping and discrepancy modeling for censored bifidelity GPs
papers.authors: Jialei Chen; Simon Mak; V. Roshan Joseph; Chuck Zhang
papers.research_question: Physical responses can exceed an instrument limit and become censored, while a cheap computer model differs from the actual physical response. The study combines both information sources to select physical experiments sequentially and predict the latent response, without treating a censoring limit as a complete measurement.
original_method: The original method represents the physical response as a computer-simulation process plus an independent discrepancy process, both with stationary Gaussian kernels. Exact observations enter ordinary conditioning; censored responses are integrated through a joint truncated distribution, retaining conditional means and covariances in prediction.

Integrated censored mean squared error selects each new experiment by averaging over possible complete observations and censoring events to reduce expected latent-response uncertainty. The model is refitted after each query. When only initial computer data are available, discrepancy covariance is set to zero.
our_method: We retain the same censored inference and ICMSE objective but apply a learned Beta-CDF input transformation to both processes, allowing location-dependent smoothness scales. Transformation parameters shrink toward the identity to limit flexibility with little data.

The discrepancy process additionally receives a full quadratic basis with a Gaussian coefficient prior; integrating the coefficients produces a covariance term. Parameters are learned from training observations, without true discrepancy coefficients. The added kernel uses numerical spatial integration, so this changes the model and induced selections, not just the acquisition criterion.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline is independently implemented from the journal's mathematical definitions; author code was unavailable. ICMSE uses full conditional variance, numerical truncated integration, finite multistart fitting and fixed search budgets. Bitwise reproduction of the authors' optimizer or convergence of every likelihood fit is not claimed.

experiments.label: Two-dimensional censored bifidelity regression
experiments.setup: Twelve MaxPro points on the unit square supply initial computer responses, followed by 40 physical queries. Noise standard deviation is 1 and the censoring limit is 10. Twenty paired repetitions share initial designs and query-indexed noise. Evaluation covers the full test set, including censored regions.
experiments.explanation: Final RMSE and interval scores both improve. Input warping and quadratic discrepancy jointly increase flexibility, without a complete ablation separating modeling and selection effects. The primary comparison uses the median of 20 final RMSEs; interquartile ranges describe between-repetition variation.

experiments.label: One-dimensional censored bifidelity regression
experiments.setup: Six equally spaced computer inputs on the unit interval precede 20 physical queries. Noise standard deviation is 0.1 and the censoring limit is 0.55. Twenty paired repetitions apply identical censoring rules and evaluate prediction of the noise-free latent physical mean.
experiments.explanation: Our method wins clearly. The discrepancy between the simulator and physical mean is exactly quadratic, matching the generic quadratic basis. This structural match does not extend to arbitrary discrepancy functions. The primary statistic is the median of 20 final RMSEs. Interval score, censoring fraction and runtime are auxiliary.

results_notes: Values are medians with interquartile ranges. Gain is the difference between method medians. 95% intervals use paired bootstrap.

papers.title: Posterior Predictive Design for Phase I Clinical Trials
papers.short_title: Posterior-predictive dose escalation and cross-dose final selection
papers.authors: Chenqi Fu; Shouhao Zhou; J. Jack Lee
papers.research_question: Phase-I trials adapt doses to sequential dose-limiting-toxicity observations and recommend the dose nearest a target toxicity rate after limited enrollment. This study separates allocation during treatment from the final recommendation, asking whether cross-dose borrowing improves final correct selection while retaining the original allocation rule.
original_method: Original PoP computes a posterior-predictive Bayes factor at each dose, comparing two hypotheses using the target toxicity and observed counts. A three-action loss matrix determines staying, escalation or de-escalation, with dose exclusions in the corresponding direction when evidence is strong.

The trial first titrates one patient at a time from the lowest dose, then enrolls prescribed cohorts. At the end, isotonic regression smooths dose-toxicity estimates and selects the tested dose nearest target, subject to shared excessive-toxicity screening.
our_method: We retain every allocation, exclusion, stopping and final safety-screening rule, replacing only the final recommendation. A finite mixture of 735 logistic dose-response models, indexed by target-crossing position and positive slope, is updated from all observed counts to borrow information across doses.

Each model identifies the nearest-target dose over the full dose set. Aggregated posterior probabilities select the highest-probability dose among those tested and safety-eligible. This directly minimizes correct-selection loss under the specified model rather than comparing distances of posterior-mean toxicities.
papers.baseline_implementation: PoP is reconstructed from the author manuscript and public code, retaining titration, cohort truncation and final screening. Random scenarios follow the main text, without a near-target-dose acceptance restriction in later author scripts, so scenario distributions are not identical.

papers.title: An optimal design framework for lasso sign recovery
papers.short_title: Composite-neighborhood design search for LASSO sign recovery
papers.authors: Jonathan W Stallrich; Kade Young; Maria L Weese; Byran J Smucker; David J Edwards
papers.research_question: 10.1093/jrsssb/qkaf026 In high-dimensional screening, runs are fewer than candidate factors, so designs must recover nonzero coefficients and signs as well as estimate values. Under a sparse Gaussian linear model, this study evaluates two-level designs by average LASSO sign-recovery probability, comparing a structural heuristic with expanded-neighborhood candidate screening.
original_method: Original HILS seeks large column variances and proximity to an ideal correlation matrix, producing Pareto candidates through coordinate exchanges. Each experiment starts from 50 random designs, merges their fronts and selects the final design using actual sign-recovery probability.

Recovery probability follows KKT conditions for active and inactive variables, averaging over supports and signs before maximizing over regularization parameters. The ideal correlation matrix guides search but need not be realizable by a supersaturated design.
our_method: We first run the same HILS fully, then add single-bit changes, balanced swaps, row flips and, with known signs, column flips, retaining every original candidate. Ten-factor tasks also receive limited direct probability-based local search. Final screening uses shared noise and the same criterion.

For 20 factors, construction uses sampled supports, so direct probability refinement is omitted to avoid overfitting that sample. Both methods share an accelerated scorer that converts KKT success events to regularization-parameter intervals. Differences come from returned designs, not scoring engines.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline reconstructs 50-start HILS from working-paper pages 28–32, using older author R code only for cross-checking. A fixed 201-point regularization grid and independent evaluation noise are used. Rank-deficient active submatrices score zero by a prespecified rule; this is not presented as an original-paper singular-case formula.

experiments.label: Nine runs, ten factors, unknown signs
experiments.setup: The 9×10 design has three active factors and effect magnitude 3 with unknown signs. Each method uses 50 shared starts and five paired repetitions. Final evaluation enumerates 120 supports and four representative sign patterns, with 1,024 Gaussian-noise draws per cell over 201 regularization points.
experiments.explanation: Every pair returns identical designs and full probability grids, giving a tie. The extra search finds no distinct superior candidate for this task. Average probabilities over supports and signs, maximize over the grid, then average over five repetitions. This is not the recovery rate of an operational tuning procedure.

experiments.label: Nine runs, ten factors, known positive signs
experiments.setup: The design remains 9×10 with three active effects of magnitude 3, but positive signs are known during design; the target correlation is 0.04. Five paired repetitions use 50 shared starts. Final evaluation enumerates 120 supports with 4,096 noise draws per cell and checks robustness at higher active-set size.
experiments.explanation: Three pairs select better designs from the expanded Pareto set; two are identical, producing an overall win. The returned improvements do not come from direct probability refinement and cannot be credited to that stage. Mean of repetition-level grid maxima. The five-pair interval crosses zero, so a numerical win is not claimed as significant population superiority.

experiments.label: Fourteen runs, twenty factors, known positive signs
experiments.setup: The 14×20 design has five active factors, magnitude 2 and target correlation 0.045. Fifty starts and three paired repetitions are used. Construction approximates with 128 supports; final scoring enumerates all 15,504 supports and 201 parameter values, with robustness checked at seven active factors.
experiments.explanation: Both methods return identical designs and tie. No candidate advantage emerges at this finite budget; better designs under other searches or inputs are not ruled out. Final scoring enumerates every nominal support. Construction-stage support sampling is not test-stage sampling.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Average probabilities over supports and signs, maximize over the grid, then average over five repetitions. This is not the recovery rate of an operational tuning procedure.

Experiment 2: Three pairs select better designs from the expanded Pareto set; two are identical, producing an overall win. The returned improvements do not come from direct probability refinement and cannot be credited to that stage. Mean of repetition-level grid maxima. The five-pair interval crosses zero, so a numerical win is not claimed as significant population superiority.

Experiment 3: Both methods return identical designs and tie. No candidate advantage emerges at this finite budget; better designs under other searches or inputs are not ruled out. Final scoring enumerates every nominal support. Construction-stage support sampling is not test-stage sampling.
results_interpretation: The results are one win and two ties. Expanded structural neighborhoods help candidate selection in the small known-sign task; the other two return identical designs. These are finite-budget gains of a particular search combination, not changes to the LASSO estimator or a global-optimality result.
theory: KKT-interval scoring is equivalent to checking each parameter separately. For fixed independent candidates, there are empirical-retention and uniform sampling-error bounds. These do not cover arbitrary adaptive support selection or ensure strictly better true recovery probability for every design.
limitations: Maximization over regularization is an idealized design-evaluation summary, not a guarantee that actual data choose that parameter. Journal equivalence of the working paper is unverified. Formal paired repetitions number only 5,5 and 3.

papers.title: Balanced Subsampling for Big Data With Categorical Predictors
papers.short_title: Balanced big-data subsampling and risk-based exchanges for categorical predictors
papers.authors: Lin Wang
papers.research_question: When responses are expensive to measure but categorical predictors are known for a large dataset, a small sample must be selected before observing responses. The original study improves regression information through category balance. This comparison distinguishes coefficient, average-prediction and worst-prediction risks and tests direct risk-based exchanges at equal labeling budgets.
original_method: The original method measures deviations of category and category-pair frequencies from uniformity. At fixed sample size, the balance objective becomes a sum of squared weighted category agreements between rows. Starting from a random row, it greedily selects from every remaining original row to minimize cumulative imbalance.

Theory connects strength-two orthogonal arrays with favorable information matrices. Simulations use treatment-coded linear regression. Real e-commerce data retain eight categorical predictors and use cross-validated LASSO after subsampling to predict the full dataset.
our_method: Starting from each paired baseline sample, we replace selected rows with unselected rows only when a weighted trace of the inverse information matrix decreases. The first two experiments directly optimize coefficient A-risk; the third uses uniform full-factorial average prediction variance. Exchanges use exact gains with periodic matrix recomputation.

The real-data information matrix is rank deficient, so the design objective uses fixed regularization and minimum category-coverage counts. This regularization affects selection only, not the shared LASSO estimator. Candidate search reads no responses, test pool or cross-validation outcomes, and selected original row identities remain distinct.
papers.baseline_implementation: Without author code, the baseline independently follows the accepted manuscript's all-remaining-rows greedy rule. Simulations analytically integrate conditional risk instead of finitely repeating responses; real data actually run glmnet cross-validation. Twenty paired repetitions and fixed prediction pools are explicit evaluation settings here.

experiments.label: Coefficient estimation with independent uniform categories
experiments.setup: Generate 100,000 rows with 20 independent uniform categorical predictors having 2–21 levels, and select 500 rows. Twenty paired repetitions share data and baseline starts. At most two exchange passes use 2,048 candidates per round. Scoring is analytic conditional risk under unit noise.
experiments.explanation: Coefficient risk wins, consistent with direct trace optimization. Auxiliary worst-prediction risk increases, showing that better coefficient estimation does not improve every predictive criterion. Each risk is the trace of the inverse treatment-coded information matrix, averaged over 20 repetitions; it is not a finite average of random-response errors.

experiments.label: Coefficient estimation with independent nonuniform categories
experiments.setup: Retain 100,000 rows, 20 factors and a 500-row subsample, but make each factor's level probabilities proportional to 1,…,q. Twenty paired repetitions use the same two-pass, 2,048-candidate exchanges to examine frequency imbalance.
experiments.explanation: Coefficient risk decreases and wins, but auxiliary maximum prediction risk worsens slightly. Direct risk selection suits the primary target without comprehensively dominating balanced subsampling. The across-seed mean of analytic conditional risk, with noise variance fixed at 1.

experiments.label: Worst-case prediction with correlated categories
experiments.setup: Discretize Gaussian variables with pairwise correlation 0.5 to generate data of the same size and select 500 rows. Twenty paired repetitions exchange for uniform average prediction variance. After selection, independently generate one million evaluation points and take their maximum conditional prediction risk.
experiments.explanation: The sampled maximum decreases and wins empirically. Theory guarantees only descent of an average-risk proxy; improvement of the maximum must be supported by these runs, not inferred directly from that proxy. Take the maximum risk over each independent million-point pool, then average over 20 repetitions. This is not the strict supremum over the full factorial space.

experiments.label: LASSO subsampling for e-commerce price prediction
experiments.setup: Retain all 165,474 public UCI rows and eight predictors, select 2,000 rows and fit shared ten-fold glmnet. Twenty paired repetitions use a single 1,024-candidate exchange pass and category-coverage constraints. Price prediction is evaluated on the entire population.
experiments.explanation: LASSO prediction error decreases and wins. Regularized design objectives and coverage protection change together; without ablation the gain cannot be assigned solely to coverage. Compute MSPE over every original row within a run, then average over 20 repetitions. Fitting uses responses only from selected rows.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use paired bootstrap.

Auxiliary worst-prediction risk increases, showing that better coefficient estimation does not improve every predictive criterion. Each risk is the trace of the inverse treatment-coded information matrix, averaged over 20 repetitions; it is not a finite average of random-response errors.

Experiment 2: Coefficient risk decreases and wins, but auxiliary maximum prediction risk worsens slightly. Direct risk selection suits the primary target without comprehensively dominating balanced subsampling. The across-seed mean of analytic conditional risk, with noise variance fixed at 1.

Experiment 3: The sampled maximum decreases and wins empirically. Theory guarantees only descent of an average-risk proxy; improvement of the maximum must be supported by these runs, not inferred directly from that proxy. Take the maximum risk over each independent million-point pool, then average over 20 repetitions. This is not the strict supremum over the full factorial space.

Experiment 4: LASSO prediction error decreases and wins. Regularized design objectives and coverage protection change together; without ablation the gain cannot be assigned solely to coverage. theory: Exact exchanges ensure nonincreasing chosen weighted trace and positive definiteness. No corresponding necessary-descent theorem covers the third task's maximum risk or the fourth task's LASSO error.
limitations: Author code and equivalence to the final journal version are unverified. The third experiment evaluates maximum risk only on its fixed million-point pool. Real-data design regularization does not guarantee lower population LASSO error.

papers.title: Complete Consecutive Order-Pairing Design and Its Distance-Based Linear Model: Design Construction and Analysis for Order-of-Addition Experiments
papers.short_title: Consecutive-component-pair designs and distance-model order optimization
papers.authors: Jing-Wen Huang; Frederick Kin Hing Phoa
papers.research_question: Order-of-addition experiments seek good component permutations from few observations, sometimes jointly with component levels. The original work builds initial designs by balanced coverage of consecutive ordered pairs and predicts candidates through distance regression. This comparison asks whether fitting unknown parameters of a published response mechanism improves confirmation choices at a limited budget.
original_method: CCOP designs balance every directed adjacent pair of distinct components and its level combinations. For even component counts, cyclic construction achieves a small run count. DBLM regresses on order distances from each candidate to the initial points, expressing similarity through adjacent-pair and level matching.

After initial observations, the model is fitted once, the best predicted batch is listed, and these candidates are confirmed before returning the best observed response. Previously measured candidates use cached values without replacement queries, so not every confirmation slot becomes a new observation.
our_method: For the two-level simulation, the published addition/subtraction/multiplication/division mechanism is used. Separable nonlinear least squares and variable projection estimate unknown operation coefficients from the 16 permitted initial observations, then confirm the 16 best predicted unobserved candidates.

The method reads neither hidden coefficients, random seeds nor all candidate responses. Failed residual checks trigger fallback to a sequential distance model. Single-level public tables have only four initial observations, and validation did not support replacement models, so both fixed-table tasks retain the original batch DBLM policy.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline is independently implemented from the publisher preprint, without author code. The two-level distance matrix has rank 12, preventing the original ordinary inverse; SVD minimum-norm fitting is prespecified. Missing printed characters in the single-level design are resolved using the full formula.

experiments.label: Four-operation, two-level simulation
experiments.setup: Four components with two levels give 384 candidates. One hundred independently generated response surfaces are each maximized and minimized. Each direction uses 16 CCOP initial points and 16 confirmation slots, at most 32 distinct observations. Both methods share surfaces and initial designs.
experiments.explanation: Our method finds the optimum in every objective stratum and wins. It uses the public mechanism and more fully spends the query allowance. Existing experiments do not isolate mechanism knowledge, fitting or additional-observation count. Average maximizing and minimizing ranks within a surface, then average 100 surfaces. Best-selection rate and regret are auxiliary.

experiments.label: Bidirectional selection on 24 fixed order responses
experiments.setup: All 24 Y1 order responses in public Table 1 are used. CCOP and CCOP* four-point starts are each maximized and minimized, giving four strata. Each adds at most three observations. There are no independent dataset repetitions.
experiments.explanation: Both methods use the same single-level policy and find the table's maximum and minimum, giving a tie. Agreement on this table does not extend to other experiments with unknown mechanisms. Average ranks equally across two initial designs and two directions. N=1 fixed table is not four independent datasets.

experiments.label: Maximizing 24 drug-response orders
experiments.setup: All 24 Y2 observations in public Table 1 are used for maximization only. CCOP and CCOP* four-point starts each permit at most three new observations. Evaluation retains original observed values without assuming true means or adding biological replications.
experiments.explanation: Both methods achieve observed ranks 1 and 2 under the two starts, giving equal averages and a tie. This is replay of a published drug-response table, not evidence of better clinical effects. Average observed ranks over the two initial designs only. True Y2 means are unknown, so this is not a true-mean ranking.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 1: Our method finds the optimum in every objective stratum and wins. It uses the public mechanism and more fully spends the query allowance. Existing experiments do not isolate mechanism knowledge, fitting or additional-observation count. Average maximizing and minimizing ranks within a surface, then average 100 surfaces. Best-selection rate and regret are auxiliary.

Experiment 2: Both methods use the same single-level policy and find the table's maximum and minimum, giving a tie. Agreement on this table does not extend to other experiments with unknown mechanisms. Average ranks equally across two initial designs and two directions. N=1 fixed table is not four independent datasets.

Experiment 3: Both methods achieve observed ranks 1 and 2 under the two starts, giving equal averages and a tie. This is replay of a published drug-response table, not evidence of better clinical effects. Average observed ranks over the two initial designs only. True Y2 means are unknown, so this is not a true-mean ranking.
results_interpretation: The three experiments yield one win and two ties. Simulation gains require a known operation class and coefficients estimable from observations; the two single-level table replays keep the original policy. Results support mechanism information for this simulation, not general superiority for unknown biological mechanisms.
theory: Finite instances have exact coverage, rank and convex-hull certificates. The distance-vector convex hull constrains fitted training values only, not the range of raw responses. Small variable-projection training residuals do not replace a global-identifiability proof.
limitations: The simulation uses a public operation mechanism, a stronger assumption than general unknown-response optimization. Both real-table tasks use fixed datasets. Final-journal and author-code equivalence are unverified.

papers.title: Locally Optimal Designs for Estimating One or More Functions of Shared Parameters Between Two Groups in Biomedical Studies
papers.short_title: Locally optimal designs and certificates for two-group shared-parameter models
papers.authors: Xin Liu; Rong-Xian Yue; Weng Kee Wong
papers.research_question: For two biomedical regression models sharing some parameters, allocation across doses depends on the function or contrast to be estimated. At fixed group proportions and nominal parameters, this study compares direct optimization with conic search and checks how far returned designs remain from continuous-dose-domain optima.
original_method: The original work builds a common two-group information matrix. It uses c-optimality for one function and weighted composite-c or L-criteria for multiple functions, targeting estimation variance. An equivalence theorem checks local optimality through sensitivity over the full dose interval.

Numerically, EMAX effective-dose differences use direct optimization over a given low-dimensional support family; exponential-model AUC differences use suggested particle-swarm search. Simultaneous extrapolated-response contrasts minimize their summed variances. All designs depend on prespecified model parameters.
our_method: We first solve a second-order cone program with fixed group masses on 61 dose points per group, then use continuous sensitivity to add doses and refine support positions and weights. An analytic estimable boundary candidate is also constructed for the AUC contrast, avoiding reliance solely on numerical search near singularity.

Returned designs are rescored by the common variance definition. Dual lower bounds and interval upper bounds assess continuous optimality. Optimized scaling tightens the displayed linear efficiency bound. Finite-grid optimality alone is not continuous-domain certification.
papers.baseline_implementation: Without author software, the EMAX and L problems use independent multistart SLSQP, and AUC uses reconstructed particle swarm. Both methods share corrections to the original AUC gradient and L-matrix dimensions. These corrections are retained; exact reproduction of every printed author result is not claimed.

experiments.label: Nine EMAX effective-dose differences
experiments.setup: Both dose ranges are 0–150, with group masses 0.2 and 0.8 and specified nominal EMAX parameters. All nine effective-dose differences p=0.1,…,0.9 are included. Each subcase has 10 seconds of search; 16 paired repetitions compare variance ratios to common reference designs.
experiments.explanation: The nine variances are nearly identical and tie. The original low-dimensional support family is already strong at these nominal parameters. Tiny numerical excursions outside the exact domain leave some returned designs uncertified. Within a run, divide each of nine variances by its reference variance and average, then average 16 runs. This is not efficiency relative to an unknown optimum.

experiments.label: Difference between exponential-curve areas
experiments.setup: Using the same dose ranges and group masses with specified exponential-model parameters, estimate the difference in AUC over 0–150. Search is limited to 40 seconds per method/run, with 16 paired repetitions. Singular information matrices are allowed if the contrast is estimable under a shared check.
experiments.explanation: Our mean is slightly lower but ties. The boundary construction and dual certificate improve numerical interpretation. The tight certificate concerns an exact symbolic representative, not automatically its rounded support points. Ratio of contrast variance to the common reference variance, averaged over 16 repetitions. Small gains do not exceed the prescribed threshold.

experiments.label: Composite estimation of three effective-dose differences
experiments.setup: Under EMAX, jointly estimate ED25, ED50 and ED75 differences with all five weight settings, including equal one-third weights. Each subcase gets 12 seconds and 16 paired repetitions. Compare weighted variance sums normalized by their reference designs.
experiments.explanation: Composite objectives are nearly identical; tiny numerical differences give ties. Changed certificate residuals or optimization formulations do not substitute for an actual variance improvement. First form the composite variance with original weights and no separate component standardization, then normalize by its reference. Average five cases equally, then seeds.

experiments.label: Joint estimation of two extrapolated response differences
experiments.setup: Observation doses remain in 0–150, but the target is the sum of variances of between-group response differences at doses 155 and 160. Both methods retain fixed group masses and the same model, with 40-second search caps and 16 paired repetitions. Estimability is checked in original coordinates.

papers.authors: Chunyan Wang; Dennis K. J. Lin
papers.research_question: Given a two-level initial design and an augmentation size, which sign-flipped foldovers reduce low-order aberration while preserving initial structure? This study compares bitwise foldover-label changes with whole-label replacement, separating attained experimental scores from optimality in restricted design classes.
original_method: The original method represents column sign flips by finite-field labels and uses the initial design's word space to identify equivalent foldovers. Vertically stacking isomorphic designs for distinct labels forms a candidate whose generalized word lengths are squared column-product sums. Search descends bitwise from random labels, then examines radius-two and radius-three perturbations at a local optimum, repeating to improve the full generalized word-length pattern. Low-order aberration has priority over higher orders, rather than an arbitrary equal-weight sum. The paper discusses multiple orderings; this comparison fixes its permitted G2 ordering.
our_method: We replace an entire foldover label, rather than one bit, to seek strict improvement in a larger legal neighborhood. Initialization mixes antipodally paired and unrestricted candidates in a 3:1 ratio. Paired starts subsequently undergo unrestricted whole-label replacement, so final search is not confined to paired families. Both arms share accelerated Walsh-kernel aberration calculations; the differences are neighborhoods and starts. The incumbent is updated only when the full generalized word-length pattern strictly improves. It always retains the best found design, but finite-time termination is not exhaustive enumeration.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline independently implements Algorithm 2: after bitwise local optimization it examines 50 radius-two and 50 radius-three perturbations from the same local optimum. Original tables mainly use G ordering. G2 is an allowed alternative, so the comparison is not a row-by-row reproduction of those tables.

papers.title: A New Class of Orthogonal Designs With Good Low Dimensional Space-Filling Properties
papers.short_title: Fine-grid projection coverage in multilevel orthogonal designs
papers.authors: Chunyan Wang; Dennis K. J. Lin; Min-Qian Liu
papers.research_question: Numerical orthogonality removes linear correlation but does not ensure uniform two-dimensional projections on fine grids. With rows, columns, levels and groups fixed, this study asks whether more column pairs can satisfy several fine-grid uniformity conditions simultaneously, and whether better overall coverage preserves the original group-specific guarantees.
original_method: The original method uses symbols of one orthogonal array to index rows of another and combines digits through signed rotation weights. Cancellation gives orthogonal numerical columns; four-digit, three-digit and mixed constructions produce different level counts. Beyond coarse-grid uniformity for all pairs, the proofs guarantee particular cross-group fine-grid projections and three-dimensional projections involving exactly two groups. These rely on the original digit arrangement and grouping, not merely low average correlation.
our_method: We construct positive-radix digits over a five-dimensional finite field and use ranks of prefix subspaces to test fine-grid uniformity, directly optimizing the fraction of all qualifying column pairs. Matching assigns distinct projection directions to columns to preserve orthogonality. Search uses 16 restarts, four cycles and finitely many strict-improvement scans. Dimensions, column order, group labels and level vectors are retained, but leading digits may change. Without a valid candidate with a better primary score, the original construction is kept. The objective is overall fine-grid coverage; not all original cross-group refinements are constrained.
papers.baseline_implementation: The three original algorithms are independently implemented using true finite-field arithmetic for prime-power levels, not integer modular arithmetic. Author code was unavailable. Original arrays and signed rotations are retained; every pair and required triple is verified by exact counting.

experiments.label: Four-digit, 625-level construction

experiments.explanation: AI wins, making some previously uncovered pairs uniform. experiments.explanation: The primary metric increases substantially and AI wins. Original within-group coverage has room for improvement, but preservation of all original three-dimensional uniformity involving exactly two groups is not proved. Required grids are 5×125, 25×25 and 125×5. The fraction counts all column pairs.

Original within-group coverage has room for improvement, but preservation of all original three-dimensional uniformity involving exactly two groups is not proved. Experiment 3: AI also wins, with a larger added fraction than in the first two experiments. Overall three-dimensional coverage rises, but some original two-group structural guarantees fail; these losses accompany the two-dimensional gain. results_interpretation: All three experiments improve overall fine-grid coverage, supporting direct projection optimization by finite-field rank conditions. Some original cross-group two-dimensional and two-group three-dimensional properties no longer all hold, and runtime increases. This improves the specified aggregate metric, not every aspect of the original construction.
theory: Prefix-rank conditions are necessary and sufficient for uniform grid counts, and distinct-direction matching supports orthogonality, enabling fast exact screening. Baseline retention ensures non-deterioration of the primary score in the selected instances. It does not cover original group-projection theorems that were not retained.
limitations: The original prediction-error example was not run because coefficients and coding were insufficiently specified. Only design structure is evaluated. Higher aggregate coverage sacrifices some original cross-group fine-grid and three-dimensional properties. No component ablation was performed.

papers.title: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions for Multiple Objective Optimal Regression Designs
papers.short_title: Adaptive solvers and certificates for multiobjective optimal design
papers.authors: Lucy L. Gao; Jane J. Ye; Shangzhi Zeng; Julie Zhou
papers.research_question: Several statistical-efficiency objectives cannot generally be optimized simultaneously. Observation weights must be allocated over fixed candidates, and the remaining gap of a compromise design assessed. This study compares full-grid convex optimization with progressively expanded supports, separately checking actual efficiency, feasibility and numerical optimality residuals.
original_method: The original paper represents an approximate design by nonnegative candidate weights, with information equal to the weighted sum of pointwise contributions. Experiments use efficiency-constrained single-objective optimization or maximize the worst efficiency across models or criteria. Convexity, directional derivatives and Lagrange multipliers characterize optimality. After solving for a design, a linear program finds verifying multipliers. The original verification fixes an allowed error and minimizes the multiplier sum: it checks a given tolerance rather than directly minimizing the maximum directional residual.
our_method: We first solve a restricted convex problem on a few evenly spaced candidates plus an atom representing the full-grid uniform design. Full-grid directional residuals identify points and neighbors to add. Sparse supports receive analytic-gradient refinement, with a full-grid solve restored when needed rather than checking support points alone. The verification LP minimizes the maximum residual. Candidates are selected by primary efficiency and residual, while raw unnormalized weights are recorded for feasibility checks. The emphasis is better numerical verification; a smaller residual does not substitute for improved primary efficiency.
papers.baseline_implementation: CVXPY, Clarabel and HiGHS reconstruct the authors' MATLAB/CVX problems with original grids and statistical criteria. Both methods share gradient and verification corrections. Where needed, only tolerances of the same optimization problem are tightened; no ridge regularization or design-domain changes are introduced.

experiments.explanation: Worst-model efficiencies are nearly identical and tie. experiments.setup: The design domain is the product of a two-level factor and a 201-point grid over -1 to 1, totaling 402 candidates. The model includes intercept, both main effects, their interaction and the second factor's square. Five paired seeds maximize minimum efficiency for A, E and the specified interaction-contrast c-criterion.

Their residuals cannot define a common algorithmic-accuracy multiplier. Take the minimum of the three efficiencies within each run, then average five runs. The E-criterion must handle repeated-eigenvalue eigenspaces.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 2: Worst-model efficiencies are nearly identical and tie. Adaptive support and refinement lower verification residuals, but do not produce a qualifying design-efficiency or speed advantage. Take the minimum across four model efficiencies within each run, then average five runs.

Experiment 3: The primary metric again ties. Refinement lowers directional residuals, indicating finer certificate solving, but the two verification LPs have different objectives. Their residuals cannot define a common algorithmic-accuracy multiplier. Take the minimum of the three efficiencies within each run, then average five runs. The E-criterion must handle repeated-eigenvalue eigenspaces.
results_interpretation: All three primary efficiencies tie, indicating baselines already close to optimal on these finite-grid convex problems. Adaptive support and smaller verification residuals are the main benefits; stable speedup is not observed. Stricter feasibility and floating-point error control are still needed to turn approximate certificates into rigorous ones.
theory: Convexity converts full-grid directional residuals into objective-gap upper bounds and yields a valid E-criterion subgradient representation for repeated minimum eigenvalues. This requires truly feasible weights and correct reference efficiencies. Double-precision residuals, normalization and tiny constraint deficits cannot replace these conditions.
limitations: Residuals are computed in double precision without interval-arithmetic certificates. Tiny constraint deficits remain in the first experiment. The verification LPs optimize different objectives. Smaller residuals are neither primary-efficiency wins nor a common accuracy multiplier.
