papers.title: Adaptive Grid Designs for Classifying Monotonic Binary Deterministic Computer Simulations
papers.short_title: Adaptive classification queries for monotone binary responses
papers.authors: Tian Bai; Dianpeng Wang; Kuangqi Chen; Xu He
papers.research_question: For a deterministic binary response increasing monotonically with inputs, a query can classify large regions without further sampling. This study compares nested-grid selection with volume-based selection to reduce unclassified regions at equal query budgets, distinguishing discrete road cases from continuous-input problems.
original_method: Original adaptive gridding propagates monotone labels: the orthant below a negative point is negative, and the orthant above a positive point is positive. At each step it searches unclassified points of the current nested dyadic grid, maximizing the smaller number eliminated by the two possible outcomes and breaking ties by the other elimination count. Once processed, the grid is refined. This balances discrete gains across outcomes. It differs from the paper's global-grid method and another internal-grid algorithm, whose results are not pooled into this baseline.
our_method: We retain label propagation but select by coverage of the actual unclassified region. In two dimensions, after eight original-method queries, strip areas are integrated exactly and balanced points searched. In four and six dimensions, 16,384 design-only scrambled Sobol particles approximate volume, with periodic refresh and candidate search. Road cases first use 12 original queries, then maximize worst-case elimination over every legal unknown grid point. Two-dimensional selection also uses an edge-interval heuristic. High-dimensional particles and local search reduce integration cost but lack continuous-space global-optimality guarantees.
papers.baseline_implementation: Author AG code was unavailable; the baseline independently implements nested grids, ordering and immediate label updates. Public road software comes from another framework and only constructs queryable cases; it is not original-algorithm code. Matching the road cases retains source limitations.

experiments.label: Two-dimensional analytic monotone thresholds
experiments.setup: A two-dimensional monotone arctangent family uses thresholds uniformly drawn from 0.92–2.10. One hundred paired repetitions each make 100 queries. An independent 100,000-point test set estimates remaining unknown volume; design points do not serve as test samples.
experiments.explanation: AI wins, consistent with exact area calculation using the continuous unknown region more directly. Balanced and edge selection change together, so their separate contributions are not identified. Each threshold yields a fraction, averaged over 100 paired repetitions.

experiments.label: Four-dimensional analytic monotone thresholds
experiments.setup: Extend the function to four dimensions, with thresholds uniform over 2.14–3.75. One hundred paired repetitions each use 360 queries and an independent 100,000-point evaluation cloud. Our method uses 16,384 design particles refreshed every 32 queries.
experiments.explanation: The mean decreases slightly but not beyond the relative threshold, giving a tie. Particle approximation and candidate search do not deliver a sufficiently large primary gain at this size. Estimate unknown volume in each repetition, then average. Design particles and test points are independent.

experiments.label: Six-dimensional analytic monotone thresholds
experiments.setup: A six-dimensional arctangent family uses uniform thresholds over 3.43–5.4. One hundred paired repetitions each make 540 queries and use an independent 100,000-point test cloud. Design still uses 16,384 particles and local search.
experiments.explanation: AI wins, showing measurable gains from more direct volume selection on the tested instances. Runtime increases, so the same advantage at equal wall-clock time is not established. Equal average of 100 volume fractions, without reweighting by the number of unknown points.

experiments.label: Discrete-grid classification of road risk
experiments.setup: Forty public road cases with nonconstant responses each have a 67×15 grid, totaling 1,005 legal inputs, and 30 queries. Twenty design seeds each traverse all 40 cases. Scoring uses the actual unknown fraction over the full discrete grid.
experiments.metric: Mean unclassified fraction across road cases
experiments.explanation: The methods tie. Our mean is slightly higher but within the absolute threshold. A one-step worst-case-elimination guarantee does not ensure a smaller final unknown fraction after all budgeted queries. Average 40 cases within each seed, then 20 seeds. This is a discrete fraction, not continuous area.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 1: AI wins, consistent with exact area calculation using the continuous unknown region more directly. Balanced and edge selection change together, so their separate contributions are not identified. Each threshold yields a fraction, averaged over 100 paired repetitions.

Experiment 2: The mean decreases slightly but not beyond the relative threshold, giving a tie. Particle approximation and candidate search do not deliver a sufficiently large primary gain at this size. Estimate unknown volume in each repetition, then average. Design particles and test points are independent.

Experiment 3: AI wins, showing measurable gains from more direct volume selection on the tested instances. Runtime increases, so the same advantage at equal wall-clock time is not established. Equal average of 100 volume fractions, without reweighting by the number of unknown points.

Experiment 4: The methods tie. Our mean is slightly higher but within the absolute threshold. A one-step worst-case-elimination guarantee does not ensure a smaller final unknown fraction after all budgeted queries. Average 40 cases within each seed, then 20 seeds. This is a discrete fraction, not continuous area.
results_interpretation: The four comparisons give two wins and two ties, with gains in two- and six-dimensional analytic problems. Road tasks show no gain; even an exact one-step criterion can be limited by remaining budget and current labels. The target is unclassified-region size, not classifier test accuracy or improved real-world road safety.
theory: Monotonicity rigorously validates label propagation. Worst-case elimination on a complete finite grid yields a one-step contraction bound, not universal final-budget dominance over the baseline. Adaptive high-dimensional particles also fail the assumptions of a simple iid error bound.
limitations: Case-by-case equivalence of public road inputs and response coding to the authors' experiments is unconfirmed. The icebreaker application lacks usable simulation-query access and has extremely high per-call cost, so it was not run. High-dimensional particles lack continuous-volume error certificates.

papers.title: Constructing orthogonal minimally aliased response surface designs using circulant weighing matrices
papers.short_title: Construction and projection optimization of weak-aberration response-surface designs
papers.authors: Nam-Ky Nguyen; Stella Stylianou; Tung-Dinh Pham; Mai Phuong Vuong
papers.research_question: 10.1080/00224065.2025.2581890 With limited runs, response-surface designs balance orthogonal main effects, estimable second-order effects and efficient low-dimensional projections. Starting from circulant weighing matrices, this study compares random construction with joint local search and column-subset optimization under common budgets and strict feasibility requirements.
original_method: Original COMARS combines circulant cores containing zeros and ±1 into a weighing matrix with orthogonal columns, selects columns, and joins them with a zero center and reversed rows. Search descends by swaps, then sign flips, restarting after stagnation; dimension reduction chooses random column subsets. Candidates satisfy rank, variance and related conditions for main-effect-plus-square models, and are ranked by the proportion of estimable full second-order projections, average D-efficiency and auxiliary aberration. Singular projections count as zero in average efficiency; only successful fits cannot be averaged.
our_method: We examine swaps and sign flips jointly within each descent, with limited perturbations of circulant cores. When reducing columns, a full projection-score table for the current matrix supports exact column exchanges instead of random subsets alone. Full two-core designs are deduplicated using proved sign, cyclic-shift and exchange equivalences; reduced and four-core designs do not use this reduction. Both arms share exact incremental scoring and eligibility checks, retaining the best eligible candidate under the finite budget without enumerating all weighing matrices.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline independently implements random cores, swap-then-flip search and random column choice from the author manuscript. Its catalog counts differ from other versions, which are not merged as reproduction targets. Both methods share models, thresholds and the final projection evaluator.

Exact projection scoring is useful for local optimization, without proving global optimality or eligibility of every high-dimensional projection.
theory: Proofs support block-structured incremental scoring, projection-table indexing and equivalence reduction for full two-core designs, reducing computation and repeated search. They establish correctness of those calculations and transformations, not global optimality of local descent or full-projection results from sampled estimability rates.
limitations: Catalog counts differ between the source manuscript and other versions; final-version consistency is unconfirmed. Large cases evaluate only prespecified samples, not all millions or hundreds of millions of projections.

papers.title: Systematic optimization methods for uniform designs under wrap-around L2-discrepancy
papers.short_title: Wrap-around discrepancy optimization and local refinement of uniform designs
papers.authors: Liangwei Qi; Changxing Ma; Yongdao Zhou
papers.research_question: High-dimensional uniform designs seek even coverage while balancing each column's levels. The original number-theoretic method rapidly generates designs. This study measures further squared wrap-around discrepancy reduction from optimizing generators, deleted columns and level arrangements while preserving dimensions and level counts.
original_method: Original systematic optimization selects constructions by sample and level counts: generalized good-lattice blocks for prime powers, power-form lattice points for larger sizes, transposed orthogonal arrays, and truncations of nearby prime-sized parent designs. Candidates usually come from contiguous column windows and finitely many row permutations. Truncation is followed by rank restoration and level folding to balance counts. Scoring is squared wrap-around L2 discrepancy including diagonal terms. Large balanced designs are generated quickly, but fixed generators and contiguous windows explore a limited candidate set.
our_method: We rerun the same original algorithm within budget and retain its output as the initial incumbent. Where finite-group structure applies, generators are optimized coordinatewise. Near-complete parent-design truncations instead optimize the few deleted columns, allowing noncontiguous retention. Finally, pair exchanges preserve every column's level counts and accept only exact objective decreases. Group structure accelerates some scores, but truncated designs are rescored from their actual matrices. Coordinatewise search follows existing ideas; this work combines and implements them for these branches rather than claiming an entirely new strategy.
papers.baseline_implementation: SOM branches are independently reconstructed from the preprint without executable author code. Some author symbol conventions remain unconfirmed. The raw squared discrepancy is evaluated without taking a square root; comparisons with other packages are not substituted for the paper baseline.

experiments.label: 197-run, 100-dimensional, full-level design
experiments.setup: Generate 197×100 with 197 levels per column, using a complete 98-column block plus a two-column remainder. Original candidates are selected from 97 contiguous windows. Ten paired seeds each get at most 60 seconds on four cores, including our initialization cost.
experiments.explanation: AI wins, but relative gains are tiny and mainly arise in balanced exchanges. A win does not imply a substantial increase in predictive accuracy. Arithmetic mean of ten squared discrepancies. The high-dimensional objective contains a large common constant, so percentage reductions are very small.

experiments.setup: Generate 289×100 with 17 levels, each repeated 17 times per column. The original method compares 45 contiguous windows of a 144-column finite-field construction. Ten paired seeds with 120 seconds and four cores compare complete balanced designs after generator optimization.
experiments.explanation: AI formally wins, with gain from generator search, but the relative change is even smaller than in other cases. This supports fine objective optimization, not reduced application error. Compare means of squared discrepancy. If seed values are identical, their sample standard deviation is zero.

papers.title: Sliced Space‐Filling Design With Mixtures
papers.short_title: Coverage and prediction optimization for sliced mixture designs
papers.authors: Zikang Xiong; Hong Qin; Yuning Huang; Jianhui Ning
papers.research_question: Mixture components sum to one, may have lower and upper bounds, and often require slices by operating condition. This study compares distribution-matching mixed-energy-distance designs with direct nearest-distance coverage optimization, evaluating overall/slice coverage and GP prediction and checking whether all uniformity criteria improve together.
original_method: Original MHED combines energy distances between the overall design, its slices and a reference distribution, balancing global and local space filling by weights. Iteration combines attraction from reference samples and repulsion among design points, updating all points by surrogate minimization. Mixtures must lie on a simplex and may have component bounds. Original unconstrained updates do not enforce these automatically. Both arms therefore solve the constrained quadratic surrogate by bounded-simplex projection and use limiting rules at coincident reference points rather than arbitrary small constants.
our_method: We directly minimize the sum of overall and slice nearest-neighbor RMS distances. Coverage centroids are weighted by inverse current group RMS distances and projected to the legal mixture region. After 500 iterations, five perturbation/refinement rounds retain only better training-coverage candidates. The two prediction tasks then expand points radially by 1.18 around the centroid and reproject. This empirical repositioning need not continue decreasing coverage loss and has no GP-error monotonicity theorem. All selections use only design-reference samples.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline independently implements original energy distance and MM, with shared constrained-projection corrections. Author files acquired later differ in some slice sizes from these prespecified instances, so pointwise design reproduction is not claimed. Prediction uses the same constant trend, anisotropic kernel and hyperparameter optimizer.

experiments.label: Unbounded three-component sliced coverage
experiments.setup: On a three-component simplex, construct three slices of 15 points, 45 total, using 10,000 training-reference and 20,000 independent test points. Twenty paired seeds each have four cores, 8 GiB and 120 seconds total, including a shared 80-second design-search cap.
experiments.metric: Sum of overall and slice RMS coverage distances
experiments.explanation: AI wins on nearest-distance coverage. Mean-representation error and minimum separation worsen, showing that coverage optimization does not simultaneously improve distribution matching and spacing. Sum RMS distances of the overall design and three slices, then average 20 seeds. This is not a sum of squared distances.

experiments.label: Sliced coverage with component bounds
experiments.setup: Three-component lower bounds are 0.10,0.05,0.15 and upper bounds 0.80,0.60,0.70. Four 15-point slices give 60 points. Use 10,000 training references, 20,000 independent test points, 20 paired seeds and the same budgets.
experiments.metric: Sum of overall and slice RMS coverage distances
experiments.explanation: The primary coverage metric improves and AI wins, showing effective direct optimization under bounded projection. Minimum spacing does not improve correspondingly, so not all space-filling criteria are better. Sum overall and four slice RMS distances within each run, then average 20 paired repetitions.

experiments.label: Prediction of three analytic responses
experiments.setup: Three 15-point slices on a three-component simplex fit polynomial, reciprocal and nonsmooth-minimum analytic responses, scored on 1,000 test points. Twenty paired seeds share GP fitting rules; design uses 10,000 reference points.
experiments.metric: Composite prediction-error metric for three responses
experiments.explanation: AI wins on the composite. All three responses improve by very different amounts, with the largest decrease for the polynomial. An approximately halved composite does not mean every response error is halved. For each response, sum overall and slice RMSEs. Take the geometric mean of those three sums within a seed, then the arithmetic mean over 20 seeds.

experiments.label: Simulated drug-mixture responses at seven doses
experiments.setup: Each of seven doses from 100 to 700 has 15 mixture points, 105 total, plus 200 test points. Component-dependent IC50 and shape parameters generate logistic responses with noise standard deviation 0.0001. Twenty paired seeds are run.
experiments.metric: Sum of overall and seven dose-specific prediction RMSEs
experiments.explanation: AI wins, supporting the combined design and radial adjustment for this simulated response. No ablation separates their contributions, and simulated predictive gain is not improved real drug efficacy. Within each run, add the overall-model RMSE and seven conditional-dose-model RMSEs, then average 20 runs.

An approximately halved composite does not mean every response error is halved. For each response, sum overall and slice RMSEs. Experiment 4: AI wins, supporting the combined design and radial adjustment for this simulated response. superiority.

papers.title: Enhanced branching Latin hypercube design and its application in automatic algorithm configuration
papers.short_title: Geometry and estimation optimization in branching Latin hypercubes
papers.authors: Bing Wen; Sumin Wang; Fasheng Sun
papers.research_question: With categorical factors, some continuous factors act only within specific categories. Ordinary Latin hypercubes do not automatically preserve uniformity inside each branch. This study retains original branching and Latin constraints while separately optimizing spacing, linear-estimation risk and sliced correlations.
original_method: Original augmented branching Latin hypercubes use combinatorial orthogonal arrays and small Latin hypercubes, with cyclic block rearrangements forming slices. With one parent category, branch-specific parts are replicated and shared factors split into coarse and fine levels. Multiple parents use symbol replacement in mixed arrays, allocating points only to occupied category combinations. Construction guarantees overall and specified branch stratification but leaves permutations within small Latin hypercubes free. Branch distances, regression estimation and correlations are distinct design objectives in the original paper.
our_method: Starting from shared random baseline components, we search exchanges preserving combinatorial and Latin structure, with 1,800 candidate evaluations per case and periodic restarts. Spacing targets branch minimum L1 distance; regression directly minimizes conditional OLS risk independent of true coefficients and responses, without test-noise access. Correlation optimization first uses signed coarse/fine correlation identities, then fine-rank swaps preserving coarse cells. Final designs need not retain the original C/G decomposition, so only proved structure and inherited correlation bounds are retained, not inapplicable identities.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline reconstructs combinatorial arrays, cyclic permutations and random Latin components from the paper. Author code and exact R random ordering are unavailable. Contrast coding for the 324-point case is completed consistently here. One hundred-run means are reported, unlike the original table's worst-of-100 summaries for some metrics.

experiments.label: Spacing at four branch-design sizes
experiments.setup: Use designs with 40,64,90 and 324 runs. The largest has 18 occupied three-parent category combinations with 18 points each. One hundred paired seeds traverse all four cases, with 20 seconds total per seed on one core and 2 GiB, and 1,800 objective evaluations per case.

Baseline errors are skewed and some seeds do not improve; a mean reduction does not promise better estimation in every run. Divide each case's squared coefficient error by parameter count, average the four cases equally within a seed, then average 100 seeds.

experiments.setup: Compare 27×3 with three slices, 64×4 with four, 108×6 with six, and 125×5 with five. Shared random constructions undergo structural exchanges and at most 5,000 fine-rank exchanges over 100 paired seeds, with overall and sliced Latin properties checked.

papers.authors: Bo Hu; Yaping Wang; Fasheng Sun
papers.research_question: Blocked definitive screening designs must estimate main effects and pure quadratics while controlling block effects. The original paper already greatly simplifies optimal allocation. This study derives an explicit odd-factor information determinant for direct integer selection of the best class and clarifies the design domain of that optimality.
original_method: Original designs combine a conference matrix, its negatives and center points. Antipodal run pairs stay in the same block, eliminating some information cross-terms. The model has intercept, main effects, pure quadratics and fixed block contrasts, without two-factor interactions. For even factor counts every block has a center, and the original theorem gives equal determinants for all permitted allocations, eliminating search. With odd factors, a vertex pair and one center-free block give two exchange classes. The original algorithm constructs and scores one representative of each and selects the more efficient; it is already simpler than earlier exhaustive B-JN search.
our_method: We retain the even-factor construction and derive the odd-case determinant. If the center-free block contains s run pairs and v indicates whether its vertex pair is in that block, the determinant is 2^(2m+1) b² m^m (s-mv)². Comparing s² with (m-s)² selects the better class, implemented by at most one swap and one full design construction/scoring. An integer certificate records both class values and the attained bound. Formal scores still come from actual model matrices; certificates neither replace evaluation nor turn ties into wins.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline faithfully implements the 2025 paper: return the initial valid allocation for even factors, compare two actual candidates for odd factors. A printed center-point error and conflicting initial-efficiency statement are corrected under a shared model. Historical exhaustive-search cost is not assigned to this baseline.

papers.title: Orthogonal Latin hypercube designs with hidden low-dimensional projection
papers.short_title: Factor capacity and fine-projection extensions of orthogonal Latin hypercubes
papers.authors: Tian-fang Zhang; Yue-ru Yan; Fasheng Sun
papers.research_question: An orthogonal Latin hypercube must combine stratification in each column, orthogonality between columns, and uniform low-dimensional projections. The original finite-field rotation construction leaves some directions unused. We examine whether these directions can increase the number of factors or improve fine-grid pairwise coverage at a fixed factor count, and clarify whether the added designs still satisfy all the original theoretical claims.
original_method: The original method builds a saturated orthogonal array on all points of a finite field, assigning one column to each projective direction, and multiplies groups of centered symbols by recursive integer rotation matrices. Distinct positional weights and independent input directions produce a complete set of Latin levels in each output column; the rotation identity ensures orthogonality between columns. Binary constructions use the S matrix, while ternary constructions use the R matrix and repeated extensions. Remaining independent directions can form an additional column. The paper also states several fine-projection properties, but some stronger counting claims fail even for actual original designs and must be checked separately from basic validity.
our_method: We verify the finite-field rank of the actual rotation support column by column, allowing valid combinations beyond the original sufficient grouping condition. In the 64-run case, six remaining directions form two columns. In the 128-run case, we fix the first 112 columns, enumerate independent triples of remaining directions, and optimize the leading digits of the final column. For ternary designs, we regroup unused directions: two additional eight-column R blocks are added at 243 runs, and classical octonion rotations produce eight-column blocks with seven-dimensional support at 2,187 runs. All added directions are distinct. We check Latin levels, exact orthogonality, and coarse-grid counts on the entire final matrix, without selecting a favorable submatrix by removing failed columns.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline independently reconstructs the paper's rotations and groupings without author code. A correction to the conflict between the R21 signs and the D10 extension is applied to both methods and is not counted as a gain. The full 64-run baseline matches the original table entry by entry; unpublished residual weights and extension orders in larger examples cannot all be confirmed.

results_interpretation: All four experiments are wins: three increase the number of usable factors, and one improves fine projections at fixed dimension. The largest example substantially raises capacity at the original run size. The contribution lies in arranging remaining directions and conducting restricted searches; the rotation matrices themselves are classical. Counterexamples exist to some original fine-projection claims, so the added designs are guaranteed only to have the properties actually verified.
theory: Exact support-rank certificates establish the Latin property of positional-weight columns. Rotation identities and distinct directions support orthogonality and coarse balance. Further results give a capacity bound and restricted optimality for the 128-run design with its fixed prefix. They do not prove that every added design retains every original fine-projection property or achieves global capacity.
limitations: Actual counterexamples exist to some stronger projection theorems in the original paper; validity under the primary metric does not imply that all those theorems hold. The authors' unpublished extension choices for larger examples could not be matched individually. The 243- and 2,187-run searches provide successful constructions, not proofs of global optimality.

papers.title: Active Learning via Heteroskedastic Rational Kriging
papers.short_title: Adaptive sampling with heteroscedastic rational kriging
papers.authors: Shangkun Wang; V. Roshan Joseph
papers.research_question: A deterministic simulator may have different amplitudes and curvatures across the input space. This study examines how to adapt kriging predictive variance to location and select simulation points sequentially to improve prediction under a fixed function-call budget, while also assessing prediction-interval reliability. Heteroscedasticity here refers to variation in the latent function, not measurement noise.
original_method: The original method builds on rational kriging, adjusting Gaussian-process scale through a positive input-dependent denominator to represent responses with varying local behavior. It first estimates the rational model's correlation lengths and mean, then optimizes scale coefficients under constraints, and finally re-estimates the mean and overall variance.

The sequential design uses maximum predictive variance. At each step, it selects a point from a newly generated candidate set reduced by twinning, obtains the true response, and refits the model. The goal is simulator prediction. Related software supplies only part of the initialization basis, rather than a ready-made implementation of the full experiments.
our_method: We retain HRK and add a positive-weight mixture model of first-order, second-order, and full-product Gaussian kernels. At each iteration, leave-one-out diagnostics on the training data select the model, allowing additive and full-interaction structures to adapt to different functions. All problems use the same selection rule.

Acquisition changes from maximum pointwise variance to integrated variance reduction. An independent set of 256 unlabeled Sobol points approximates average uncertainty, and acquisition is compared on a shared candidate set. Model selection and acquisition use only paid-for responses, with no access to the true function formula or final test labels. Ablation has not separated the individual contributions of these two changes.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline reconstructs HRK parameter estimation, latent variance, and maximum-variance acquisition from the 23-page arXiv v1; it is not replaced by ordinary kriging. Where a high-dimensional curve's starting point conflicts with its caption, the caption's 10p initial size is used. Some finite-step optimizations are not proved globally optimal.

However, both methods' interval coverage remains well below 95%, and the improved method also takes longer on average. Compare median RMSE over 10 paired repetitions, with supplementary interval scores, coverage rates, and runtime.

Experiment 2: The numerical rule gives an AI win, but only 5 pairs improve, the interval crosses zero, and the prediction-interval score worsens. The conclusion is restricted to the primary RMSE statistic. Again compare medians; means, quartiles, and intervals are supplementary descriptions.

Experiment 3: All 10 pairs improve, giving more consistent gains than the first two experiments. However, both methods' interval coverage remains well below 95%, and the improved method also takes longer on average. results_interpretation: All three experiments are wins under the prespecified median rule, with OTL showing the most consistent improvements across repetitions. The results support the predictive value of combining mixture-model selection and integrated acquisition on these tasks. The first two experiments show substantial seed uncertainty, and RMSE gains do not imply comprehensive improvements in coverage or runtime.
theory: Positive scale transformations preserve covariance validity. For a fixed model, the Schur complement gives one-step integrated variance reduction on a finite grid. This result does not cover parameter re-estimation, model selection, continuous-integration error, or actual RMSE reduction for a deterministic true function.
limitations: Experimental equivalence between the journal article and the working preprint has not been verified; the discrepancy in historical curve starting points is documented. Other simulations and the two real-data examples were not run. General calibration of prediction intervals has not been proved.

papers.title: Exact designs for order-of-addition experiments under a transition-effect model
papers.short_title: Exact order-of-addition designs under transition-effect models
papers.authors: Jiayi Zheng; Nicholas Rios
papers.research_question: When a run is defined by the order in which components are added, directed transitions between adjacent components may affect the response. This paper studies how to select complete permutations, or permutations satisfying ordered-block constraints, at a fixed run size to improve transition-effect estimation and average prediction over all feasible orders.
original_method: The original paper uses indicators of adjacent directed edges to construct the TE1 regression model, dropping one redundant transition term for identifiability. In blocked problems, only within-block transitions are retained; adjacency across blocks is excluded. The D criterion targets joint parameter estimation, while the I criterion targets average prediction variance under the uniform distribution over feasible orders.

Designs are found by GRASP. Each iteration randomly selects relatively good proposals from adjacent-swap candidates, then improves the design locally row by row, gradually reducing randomness in candidate selection. Evaluation uses the information moment over all feasible permutations as the reference, without observing responses or splitting data into training and test sets.
our_method: Under the same TE1 model and run size, we broaden the permutation neighborhood by combining within-row transpositions, directed insertions, segment reversals, and random feasible orders. Blocked problems periodically check every within-block permutation. When the feasible space is small, all candidates for a complete row are also enumerated; after stagnation, the current design is perturbed and search resumes.

Both methods share stable rank-two updates, full-rank checks, and the corrected complete reference matrix, so these common computational corrections are not counted as contributions unique to our method. The new search uses more of the available time to explore candidates while retaining the best feasible design. It does not guarantee global optimality at a finite run size.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline reconstructs the preprint's GRASP configuration of 100 iterations and 250 candidates per iteration. It initializes once and continues its state, following the author code's interpretation of ambiguous pseudocode. Normalization of the blocked reference matrix is repaired according to the original definition, with the same correction applied to both methods.

The smaller feasible space permits more complete-row enumeration, but this comparison does not equalize the actual number of proposals processed by the methods. Decide the outcome using the arithmetic mean of 20 D-efficiencies, with the same complete feasible reference for both methods.

However, our method runs longer in practice and processes more proposals. The results therefore do not establish an advantage at equal computational work, and do not cover the original paper's other algorithms and
applications.
theory: After correction of the blocked uniform matrix, permutation-group averaging establishes D/I reference optimality for the specified TE1 model. Necessary divisibility conditions on run size show that the chosen sizes cannot attain the reference matrix exactly. This neither determines the optimality gap nor proves global convergence of the search.
limitations: The study uses a 34-page preprint; full experimental equivalence with the journal version has not been verified. Actual computational work differs between methods. Length-two transitions, other search comparators, and application examples were not run.

papers.title: Sequential Designs for Filling Output Spaces
papers.short_title: Sequential coverage designs for unknown output spaces
papers.authors: Shangkun Wang; Adam P. Generale; Surya R. Kalidindi; V. Roshan Joseph
papers.research_question: 10.1080/00401706.2023.2231042 Uniform sampling in the input space need not cover a simulator's outputs, especially when attainable outputs lie on a curved manifold or arise from a narrow active input region. This paper studies how observed input–output pairs can guide sequential filling of output-space gaps, and whether the resulting samples improve nearest-neighbor inverse lookup for robot target positions.
original_method: The original OSFD method approximates Voronoi cells of observed outputs, using local simplices, nearest-neighbor midpoints, and samples inside balls to find uncovered locations. When output dimension exceeds input dimension, local principal-component tangent spaces approximate the output manifold, and output scaling is updated with observations.

The greedy version selects a new point in the input neighborhood corresponding to the largest gap. OSFD-EI additionally constructs expected improvement from a nearest-neighbor mean and distance-dependent variance to balance exploitation and exploration. The first three simulations use EI, while the robot task uses the greedy method; EI itself is therefore not a new contribution in this comparison.
our_method: For vector outputs, a local radial basis function predicts candidate outputs. Their distance from the observed output set measures novelty, supplemented by a prediction-disagreement penalty and input exploration. Multiscale candidates seek narrow active regions, while a small amount of independent exploration retains access to uncovered input regions.

For scalar outputs, paid-for search first seeks the edges of the observed range, followed by safeguarded interpolation queries targeting the largest output gap. All boundary queries count against the shared budget. The method does not use true extrema, analytic inverses, or the evaluation grid, and a cap on queries for an individual search can stop it before the target tolerance is reached.
papers.baseline_implementation: OSFD-EI and OSFD-greedy are reconstructed from the 36-page preprint. A publisher appendix obtained later supports the core steps, but the external R package and some tutorial settings differ from the frozen implementation. Point-for-point reproduction of the authors' software or all journal experiments therefore cannot be claimed.

experiments.label: Coverage of the two-dimensional inverse-radius output
experiments.setup: Map two-dimensional inputs to inverse radius and angle. Start both methods from the same 10-point random LHD and expand to 150 points over 20 paired repetitions. Compute fill distance on a prespecified 1,001 × 1,001 grid over the closure of the attainable output set, avoiding evaluation only on uniformly sampled inputs.
experiments.explanation: All 20 pairs improve. Direct prediction of output gaps is consistent with the improvement direction, but no ablation separates the contributions of the RBF model, candidate strategy, and exploration. Take the arithmetic mean of fill distances over 20 runs. Each is a maximum nearest-neighbor distance on a fixed grid, not a certified supremum over the continuous domain.

experiments.label: Coverage of a three-dimensional exponential output manifold
experiments.setup: Two-dimensional inputs generate three-dimensional outputs with exponential coefficients 100, 200, and 400. Expand 50 initial points to 1,000 over 10 paired repetitions. Evaluate output-manifold coverage on 1,002,001 grid pairs constructed in transformed coordinates, with the same function-call budget for both methods.
experiments.explanation: All 10 pairs improve, indicating fuller coverage on this problem with a strongly localized active region. Longer computation and changes in both the surrogate and candidates may contribute to the result. Take the arithmetic mean over 10 runs using distances in the original three-dimensional output coordinates. The target set measures coverage of the effective output region, rather than average prediction error under uniform inputs.

experiments.label: Scalar-output coverage of the eight-dimensional Easom function
experiments.setup: Use the modified eight-dimensional Easom function, retaining the exponential term inside the product over dimensions. Start from 200 shared points and sample up to 1,000 over 10 paired repetitions. Use the verified full output interval to calculate endpoint omissions and the largest internal half-gap.
experiments.explanation: All 10 pairs improve, mainly through smaller omissions at the lower and upper endpoints; internal gaps dominate the remaining error. Large baseline errors represent real undercoverage and were not removed as failed runs. Average the exact interval distances over 10 runs. Larger endpoint omissions in a few repetitions produce substantial between-run variation.

experiments.label: End-effector inverse lookup for a four-link robot
experiments.setup: The robot has four link lengths and four angles, giving eight input dimensions and two end-effector output dimensions. Start from the same 30-point LHD selected by a maximin candidate criterion and expand to 300 points over 20 paired repetitions. Evaluate nearest-neighbor inverse-lookup error on 100,030 fixed disk targets.
experiments.metric: Mean across runs of average inverse-lookup error
experiments.explanation: Mean inverse-lookup error improves in 19 pairs, and supplementary upper-quantile errors also decrease. Not every target or repetition improves, and the result depends on the fixed target distribution. First average distances over the fixed target set, then take the arithmetic mean over 20 repetitions. Paired intervals do not include uncertainty from target sampling.

papers.title: Designs for Order-of-Addition Screening Experiments
papers.short_title: Order-of-addition screening designs with a fixed subset size
papers.authors: Zack Stokes; Hongquan Xu
papers.research_question: When more components are available than can be added in one run, both a fixed-size subset and its order must be selected. This paper studies compact designs that support estimation of these effects and applies them to job scheduling with completion-time costs, assessing design efficiency and the number of queries needed to find the optimal sequence.
original_method: The paper proposes the component-position screening (CPS) and pairwise-order screening (PWOS) models; PWOS assigns zero to component pairs that do not both appear. The complete ordered-subset design provides a D-optimal reference for both models, and smaller designs are constructed using component orthogonal arrays and order orthogonal arrays.

The scheduling application first runs the constructed design, then fits a CPS linear model and maximizes expected improvement over unqueried sequences. The response is a quadratic cost of cumulative completion times plus a rejection penalty; the selected sequential experiments use zero rejection penalty. Screening here means selecting and ordering components, rather than testing for significant variables.
our_method: For fixed designs, we start from the original construction, perform exact row exchanges, and compare the result with searches from two random starts. Every accepted move is checked for an increase in the unregularized determinant, and the best design is retained. This directly optimizes the selected CPS or PWOS objective without guaranteeing simultaneous gains for other models.

For scheduling, we use the publicly specified quadratic response family, fitting nonnegative latent processing times and costs from queried responses, then querying the sequence with the lowest predicted cost. Scale normalization mitigates parameter nonuniqueness without using hidden true parameters. This incorporates more structural knowledge than generic CPS and consequently has a narrower scope.
papers.baseline_implementation: COA/OA constructions and CPS-EI are implemented from the 21-page journal article and 11-page supplement. Prespecified conventions address unspecified details of the column-permutation objective, prediction standard errors, and tie breaking. Author code is unavailable, so full software equivalence cannot be claimed.

experiments.explanation: The primary CPS efficiency improves, giving a win, while supplementary PWOS efficiency decreases. This is an improvement in the selected model's objective, not simultaneous support for every model. Take the arithmetic mean over 10 runs. The baseline construction is deterministic; repetitions measure randomness in our search.

A value numerically close to one does not prove exact global optimality. Take the arithmetic mean over 10 runs. The selected 120-run design is not the full 672-run construction covered by the original optimality guarantee.

experiments.setup: Use the public processing times and costs for seven jobs, with all 5,040 sequences available. Query 41 shared initial points, then 100 additional points per method. The 10 repetitions relabel the same instance; they are not 10 independent scheduling tasks.

papers.title: On Construction of Nonregular Two-Level Factorial Designs With Maximum Generalized Resolutions
papers.short_title: Nonregular two-level designs with maximum generalized resolution
papers.authors: Chenlu Shi; Boxin Tang
papers.research_question: Strength-two orthogonal two-level designs eliminate confounding among main effects, but higher-order confounding still depends on the construction. This paper studies how to reduce the largest three-column J-characteristic at fixed run and factor counts, thereby increasing generalized resolution, and whether existing tensor constructions leave room for improvement.
original_method: Starting from Paley designs and Hadamard matrices, the paper uses tensor products and recursive constructions to produce large strength-two orthogonal arrays and gives lower bounds for the largest three-column J-characteristic. Generalized resolution is determined by the ratio of the largest absolute three-column J to the run count. Smaller maximum absolute J means weaker worst-case third-order confounding and higher generalized resolution.

The constructions apply at different sizes: tensor products of two OAs, recursive Hadamard–OA tensor products, and a second Paley-type construction. Some examples attain a general lower bound; others provide only feasible designs. These are combinatorial objects requiring no response data, so repeated execution does not produce new independent experimental data.
our_method: We first construct and score the original design exactly, retaining it immediately if it attains the general lower bound. For the 384 × 341 problem, where a theoretical gap remains, we additionally generate several parent constructions, project them to the required factor count, and use closed-quadruple row switches to explore other strength-two arrays.

The switches group characters on four rows to preserve the full column Gram matrix, retaining balance and pairwise orthogonality. Search selects improvements using the three-column J histogram and retains the best matrix starting from the original design. A generic integer scorer finally enumerates every triple, rather than replacing actual evaluation with tensor formulas or reported paper values.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline implements the Paley, tensor, and recursive constructions formula by formula from the verified 15-page journal paper, preserving the original dimensions and H4 signs. Both methods check all one-, two-, and three-column J-characteristics. Historical author code was not obtained, but the required mathematical constructions can be checked directly.

papers.title: A Position-Based Approach for Design and Analysis of Order-of-Addition Experiments
papers.short_title: Multi-model order-of-addition design and prediction with position models
papers.authors: Zack Stokes; Hongquan Xu
papers.research_question: Order-dependent responses can be modeled through pairwise precedence or component positions, but a limited run budget may not identify the best model in advance. This paper studies exact order-of-addition designs accommodating multiple position models and uses public five-drug combination data to assess position-effect prediction for responses held out of the training folds.
original_method: The paper compares pairwise-order and component-position models with first-order, pure-quadratic, and second-order polynomial models of positions, using discrete orthogonal polynomials for position coding. After finite-field constructions generate candidate designs, permutations of component columns improve the geometric mean of D-efficiencies across models, yielding the common design F*.

The public drug application contains 40 observations in two batches. The original analysis includes batch effects, linear and quadratic position effects, and position interactions as candidates for bidirectional AIC stepwise regression. Design evaluation requires no responses, while prediction requires model refitting; conclusions from these tasks are not interchangeable.
our_method: For design, we start from the recomputed F* and apply complete-row exchanges, perturbations, and restarts to a joint normalized log-determinant objective across models, always retaining the best feasible design. This can improve composite efficiency without requiring every model, balance measure, or confounding measure to improve simultaneously.

For prediction, we use grouped ridge regression over a component-symmetric dictionary. Within each outer training fold, exact leave-one-out PRESS for fixed penalties selects the tuning parameters, followed by prediction of held-out observations. Model selection never uses outer test responses, nor does it reuse variables or coefficients fitted on the full data.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline reconstructs the finite-field construction from the journal article and exhausts all column permutations, using F* rather than the weaker unpermuted design. The drug baseline repeats AIC selection within each training fold. Because unspecified construction ordering is fixed by convention, the seven-component results need not match every numerical entry of the original table.

experiments.label: Four run sizes for five components
experiments.setup: Construct designs from all 120 permutations of five components, with 20, 24, 40, and 60 runs and no duplicate rows. Evaluate five models at each size: PWO, CP, FO, PQ, and SO. Ten repetitions cover the full set of sizes under a shared 30-second limit.
experiments.explanation: Composite efficiency gives a win, with gains mainly at 24 and 60 runs. Other sizes are unchanged, and supplementary balance measures may worsen; not all design properties improve. First take the geometric mean of model-specific D-efficiencies, then the arithmetic mean across the four sizes, and finally the mean over 10 runs.

experiments.label: Six run sizes for seven components
experiments.setup: Select 24, 36, 48, 60, 84, and 120 distinct runs from 5,040 permutations of seven components. Ten repetitions share a 180-second limit. Models enter the score at each size only when their prespecified parameter count does not exceed the run count.
experiments.explanation: Mean efficiency increases, mainly through gains at 24 and 36 runs; the least efficient model also improves. Some W1 and W2 values worsen, so a win on the primary metric does not imply uniformly reduced confounding. Take the geometric mean over the fixed eligible model set, then arithmetic means across six sizes and 10 runs. An eligible model with deficient rank scores zero.

experiments.label: Held-out prediction for 40 five-drug observations
experiments.setup: Use all 40 real observations in the original table, 20 from each batch. Each repetition has five outer folds, each holding out four observations per batch and training on 32, with 10 paired split configurations. Stepwise selection and ridge tuning use only the corresponding training fold.
experiments.explanation: The prespecified tolerance gives a win, with improvement in eight of the 10 splits, but the paired interval crosses zero. This supports a numerical improvement in internal validation, not a clear external predictive advantage. Pool the 40 out-of-fold predictions to calculate RMSE in each repetition, then average over 10 split configurations. Repeated splits reuse the same data.

Experiment 2: Mean efficiency increases, mainly through gains at 24 and 36 runs; the least efficient model also improves. Some W1 and W2 values worsen, so a win on the primary metric does not imply uniformly reduced confounding. Experiment 3: The prespecified tolerance gives a win, with improvement in eight of the 10 splits, but the paired interval crosses zero. This supports a numerical improvement in internal validation, not a clear external predictive advantage. Pool the 40 out-of-fold predictions to calculate RMSE in each repetition, then average over 10 split configurations. Repeated splits reuse the same data.
results_interpretation: All three experiments are wins on the prespecified primary metrics. Higher composite design efficiency does not guarantee benefits for every model or balance measure. The drug-prediction gain is small and its interval crosses zero. These results support further evaluation of the design and regularization combinations, but not conclusions about new batches, unobserved sequences, or clinical efficacy.
theory: Exact exchange updates, baseline retention, and concavity upper bounds for composite log-determinants hold for a fixed objective. The PRESS identity applies only to a fixed penalty; it does not automatically account for the additional adaptivity cost of choosing that penalty.
limitations: Design gains involve more actual computation, and some balance and confounding measures deteriorate. Drug-related conclusions come only from repeated internal validation on the same 40 observations. Equivalence to the authors' software has not been verified.

papers.title: Active Learning of Piecewise Gaussian Process Surrogates
papers.short_title: Boundary learning and sampling for piecewise Gaussian processes
papers.authors: Chiwoo Park; Robert Waelder; Bonggwon Kang; Benji Maruyama; Soondo Hong; Robert B. Gramacy
papers.research_question: A single stationary Gaussian process struggles to represent a discontinuous response, and incorrect region assignments can distort both predictive bias and uncertainty. This paper studies learning piecewise boundaries in local neighborhoods and guiding sampling with both bias and variance. The present experiments focus on prediction error for two regions separated by a linear boundary.
original_method: The original JGP method takes a local neighborhood around each prediction point, uses an affine classifier to separate same-region observations from an outside group, and fits local latent variables and a Gaussian process by classification EM. Prediction uses only the selected group, with the mean estimated by generalized least squares.

Acquisition maximizes estimated mean squared prediction error: squared bias derived from the regional mean difference and classification probabilities, plus latent variance under an approximate membership configuration. The selected baseline retains 15 nearest neighbors and the R = 0 configuration approximation. The paper also proposes integrated acquisition, but it is not the baseline here.
our_method: We pool observed data into two global GP experts, divide regions using a learned affine gating function, and refine assignments through leave-one-out response likelihoods. Compared with fitting a local model at each point, this shares more data within regions, at the cost of flexibility for complicated curved boundaries.

The acquisition variance includes both within-expert variance and regional uncertainty due to differences between expert means. A Laplace approximation handles uncertainty in gating parameters. Final prediction selects one expert rather than using the mixture mean. This combination suits the selected two-region problems, but offers no general guarantee of prediction-interval calibration.
papers.baseline_implementation: The baseline is reconstructed from the 35-page arXiv v4 and the CEM formulas it cites, correcting differences in metrics, neighborhoods, and budgets in public demonstration code. The MATLAB workflow obtained later is not equivalent to this baseline, so this is not a direct reproduction of that publisher-supplied software or its historical curves.

experiments.explanation: Seven pairs improve, and lower mean RMSE gives a win. Pooling data and matching the two-region structure are plausible explanations, but no ablation separates gating, expert fitting, and acquisition. Take the arithmetic mean of final RMSE over eight paired repetitions. Supplementary NLPD and CRPS do not change the outcome decision.

experiments.setup: Use a five-dimensional, two-region GP with the same mean difference and noise and a correlation length of 0.5. After 100 shared initial points, add 50 points from 500 candidates. Eight paired function repetitions use identical call counts and 1,000 noiseless test targets.
experiments.explanation: All eight pairs improve on the primary RMSE. This supports performance for the current linear two-region setting, not for multiple regions, curved boundaries, or every uncertainty score. Take the arithmetic mean over eight runs. papers.title: Batch Sequential Experimental Design for Calibration of Stochastic Simulation Models
papers.short_title: Batch exploration and replication for stochastic simulator calibration
papers.authors: Özge Sürer
papers.research_question: A stochastic simulator has both an unknown response surface and location-dependent simulation noise. Under a fixed call budget, new locations and replications at existing locations serve different purposes. This paper studies how a heteroscedastic GP can select a batch of simulations to improve the unnormalized parameter posterior defined by observed data.
original_method: The original method separately models the simulation mean and input-dependent noise, fitting a heteroscedastic GP for each output. Replicated simulations enter through their sample means, with observation-noise variance decreasing as the replication count grows. Field measurement noise, simulation noise, and surrogate predictive variance are treated separately.

Each batch compares replication and exploration proposals. Replication allocates counts using approximate variance updates; exploration selects new locations sequentially while holding predicted means fixed. Integrated posterior variance then selects one proposal. Refitting occurs only after all batch simulations are complete, without using early responses within the batch.
our_method: We add mixed replication-and-exploration proposals to the original two options. Gaussian conditioning computes expected posterior variance for the full joint batch exactly, retaining candidates that account jointly for correlations across locations and replication counts. Candidate coordinates and the simulation model are shared with the baseline, with no additional true responses.

Selection first requires that the batch variance objective be no worse than either original proposal. Marginal Monte Carlo integration then approximates expected absolute error to choose among qualifying batches. This rule is closer to the final MAD criterion, but switching at twice the standard error is a heuristic for integration stability, not a significance test.
papers.baseline_implementation: Replication/exploration and hetGP fitting are reconstructed from the 40-page preprint, with allocation signs and noise scales cross-checked against author code. The unimodal observation variance is set to 0.01 from the original PDF, rather than the different value in current author code. Both methods share fitting settings.

experiments.label: Calibration of a unimodal stochastic simulator
experiments.setup: Use a two-dimensional parameter and a scalar quadratic response with location-dependent simulation noise. Regenerate field observations for each seed. Start from 15 shared LHS locations with two simulations each, then run 16 batches of 16, totaling 286 calls. Evaluate 10 paired repetitions on a 50 × 50 grid.
experiments.explanation: Our method increases error, so the original method wins; only two pairs improve. A one-step model-variance constraint does not guarantee lower actual trajectory MAD after refitting. First average absolute errors across 2,500 points, then take the arithmetic mean over 10 repetitions. The target is the unnormalized posterior density retaining Gaussian constants.

experiments.label: Calibration of a banana-shaped stochastic simulator
experiments.setup: Use two parameters and a two-output banana-shaped mean, separating piecewise heteroscedastic simulation noise from fixed field noise. Again initialize 15 locations with two replications each, then add 256 calls. Ten paired seeds share candidates and noise paired by call index.
experiments.explanation: Seven pairs improve and the mean reduction exceeds the tolerance, giving a win. The improvement interval still crosses zero, and the individual contributions of mixed replication, exploration, and proposal selection remain undetermined. Take the arithmetic mean of 2,500-point grid MAD over 10 runs. The paired t interval only describes variation across seeds.

experiments.label: Calibration of a bimodal stochastic simulator
experiments.setup: A nonlinear two-output mean over two parameters produces a bimodal posterior; simulation noise increases with parameter-vector norm. The interval crosses zero, indicating substantial between-run uncertainty about the advantage at this budget. papers.title: Optimal Experimental Designs for Process Robustness Studies
papers.short_title: Designs for predicting response differences in process robustness studies
papers.authors: Ying Chen; Bernard G. Francq; Peter Goos
papers.research_question: Process robustness concerns how much the response changes across an operating region relative to a reference condition, rather than prediction accuracy for the response alone. This paper studies exact response-surface designs minimizing average variance of predicted differences, and how reference location, candidate levels, and random blocks affect the design.
original_method: The paper proposes the GID criterion, integrating prediction variance for the difference between a regional response and the reference response over a continuous uniform region. For a full quadratic model, it combines average prediction variance, variance at the reference point, and twice the average covariance. It therefore differs from a simple D- or I-optimal objective.

Designs are generated by coordinate exchange from random starts, repeatedly changing one factor level in one run and accepting only strict GID reductions. Random-block problems use covariance with a random intercept and the GLS information matrix. Exact polynomial moments compute regional integrals, rather than averages over candidate points.
our_method: We add integer starting designs guided by an approximate-design relaxation and perturb promising designs, combining whole-point replacement and between-block exchanges to broaden the neighborhood. Unlike coordinate moves, these operations can change several factors or block assignments simultaneously. Returned designs always preserve the specified run count and candidate levels.

Low-rank updates tailored to GID and block covariance accelerate computation, followed by direct-solve checks of the final objective. Rational global lower bounds are also generated and paired with feasible design values to assess near-optimality. Relaxed solutions guide starting points and tighten certificates; they are not treated as proofs of exact-design optimality.
papers.baseline_implementation: Multi-start coordinate search, continuous uniform integration, and random-block GLS are reconstructed from a 41-page author manuscript. Each baseline run completes more than 1,000 independent starts. The pharmaceutical reference point is rounded as in the original figure. Author code and supplementary design tables have not been obtained.

experiments.label: Three-factor design with a central reference
experiments.setup: Use a full quadratic model with three factors and 10 parameters. Select 20 runs, allowing repeats, from levels -1, 0, and 1 for each factor, with the origin as reference. Eight search repetitions share the candidate problem and a 300-second limit. GID is integrated analytically over the continuous cube.
experiments.explanation: Both methods obtain the same exact objective, giving a tie. The more complex search shows no benefit, but the current lower bound is insufficient to establish global optimality of this solution. Take the arithmetic mean over eight runs. Both methods have the same exact rational value; small displayed floating-point differences are not improvements.

experiments.label: Three-factor design with a vertex reference
experiments.setup: Retain 20 runs, the three-factor quadratic model, and three-level candidates, but move the reference to (1, 1, 1). Eight repetitions compare GID search under identical resources, assessing the effect of an asymmetric reference location on design and search.
experiments.explanation: The methods tie, showing that broader neighborhoods do not further reduce difference-prediction variance in this fixed problem. The tie does not imply a lack of benefit for all reference points. Take the arithmetic mean of eight objective values. The exact rational values are identical for both methods.

experiments.label: Five-level design for the Rotarix process
experiments.setup: Construct a quadratic model in shear stress, temperature, and pH, choosing 20 runs from five levels per factor. Both construction and scoring use the rounded reference (-1, -0.5, 0), with eight repetitions. No drug-efficacy response data are read.
experiments.explanation: Both methods have identical exact GID and tie. The conclusion is limited to the shared five-level candidates and rounded reference; this is not a comparison of vaccine potency or actual process performance. Take the arithmetic mean over eight runs. Scoring uses the original table's target coding of -1; the more precise coding of the physical target is -0.96.

experiments.setup: Use a four-factor quadratic model with 15 parameters. Choose 32 runs from three-level candidates, divided into four fixed blocks of eight runs. The random-intercept variance ratio is 1 and the reference is (-1, 0, 0, 0). Eight repetitions compute GID from GLS information.

papers.title: Solving Bayesian Inverse Problems Using Gaussian Process Regression with Goal-Oriented Active Learning
papers.short_title: Goal-oriented GP sampling for Bayesian inverse problems
papers.authors: Paul Lartaud; Philippe Humbert; Josselin Garnier
papers.research_question: Surrogate error in an expensive forward model propagates into a Bayesian inverse problem, making the parameter posterior depend on training-point placement. This paper studies targeted additions of forward simulations guided by the current posterior, seeking a high-accuracy reference posterior with few calls, while distinguishing reduced surrogate uncertainty from reduced final posterior KL divergence.
original_method: The original method represents correlated outputs with a linear model of coregionalization GP, incorporating both the noise covariance of averaged observations and shared surrogate error into the likelihood. IP-SUR weights by the current parameter posterior and minimizes the integrated determinant of predictive covariance after a new observation, refining regions relevant to the inverse problem.

At each iteration, Adaptive Metropolis samples approximate the posterior integral, followed by acquisition optimization and a forward-model call. The original theorem concerns convergence of determinant-based uncertainty, not a direct finite-budget posterior KL guarantee. Numerical comparisons use a reference posterior from an additional 1,000-point GP.
our_method: We replace the determinant objective with the trace of covariance whitened by observation noise, so that every output direction still uncertain relative to noise contributes to acquisition. The forward GP, likelihood, initial data, and function-call count match the baseline. Changes are concentrated in the acquisition objective and its numerical integration and optimization.

Integration uses 8,192 Sobol locations covering the full domain. Search combines 256 global candidates, 64 posterior-weighted candidates, and five local refinements. Global sampling helps cover regions beyond the current posterior, but a finite integration grid and local searches do not constitute ideal globally optimal acquisition.

experiments.label: Twenty refinements of a banana-shaped posterior

No accuracy or runtime advantage is observed, and a tie does not establish equivalence of the methods. Take the arithmetic mean over six runs. The reference GP and grid are used only for evaluation. The original density expression is corrected according to its GP model.

papers.title: The Traveling Bandit: A Framework for Bayesian Optimization with Movement Costs
papers.short_title: Batch Bayesian optimization with movement costs
papers.authors: Qiyuan Chen; Raed Al Kontar
papers.research_question: When an experiment requires moving equipment as well as obtaining an observation, selecting points solely for high responses can create long routes. This paper jointly considers noisy function optimization and visitation paths, seeking a balance between cumulative regret and movement cost under a limited query budget.
original_method: The original method performs GP upper-confidence-bound search in gradually increasing batches. It first determines the points in a batch, then orders their visits using an approximate traveling-salesperson route. Observations update the surrogate, while locations violating historical confidence constraints are continually excluded. The elimination threshold is the maximum lower confidence bound over the entire design domain, and every past elimination condition must be retained.

Batching connects statistical learning with equipment movement: points in a batch can be visited together to reduce back-and-forth travel. The paper further discusses route length and regret bounds in general metric spaces, but these results require geometric conditions and completion of every batch.
our_method: We retain batch generation, confidence bounds, and historical elimination conditions, replacing only the approximate route through a fixed batch with Held–Karp dynamic programming. This exactly solves the open path starting at the current location with a free endpoint. Small batches make this standard combinatorial optimization method directly usable.

For the same point set, an exact route is no longer than a candidate approximate route. However, visit order may alter observations available later and subsequent batch decisions, so this does not imply a lower combined loss for the entire learning process. Validation could not complete the corrected baseline, and the improved route produced no comparable formal scores.
papers.baseline_implementation: The GP, global threshold, persistent elimination, and approximate routing are reconstructed from the 21-page arXiv v1, with matching and Euler traversal repaired. The previously runnable version computed thresholds only on the current active set, contrary to the original definition; its historical values are excluded from comparison.

Formal scoring was not performed, so there is no mean or improvement rate.

theory: The metric h(r) = r log(e/r) provides a dimension-one counterexample whose path length grows with the number of points, showing that the general metric-space result needs additional geometric conditions. limitations: Agreement between the journal experiments and working preprint on dimension and budget is unconfirmed; some GP optimization details are independently reconstructed. papers.title: Optimal Response Surface Designs for Detection and Minimization of Model Contamination
papers.short_title: Response-surface designs balancing model bias and testing ability
papers.authors: Olga Egorova; Steven G. Gilmour
papers.research_question: Response-surface models may omit higher-order terms. More distinct treatment points help estimate the surface, while replicated observations help estimate pure error and test lack of fit. This paper studies how to allocate treatment locations and replications at a fixed total run size, balancing parameter precision, lack-of-fit testing, and bias from model contamination.
original_method: The original method combines primary-model parameter precision, lack-of-fit testing, and mean squared error including omitted-term bias in a geometrically weighted criterion. A prior scale represents potentially omitted higher-order coefficients. Replicated treatment points provide pure-error degrees of freedom, so the number of support points also affects the objective.

Multi-start point exchange searches a finite treatment candidate set for smaller criterion values. The determinant version uses the paper's specified point-prior approximation, while the trace version uses an analytic expectation under a Gaussian prior. Both represent model uncertainty, but they cannot both be interpreted as exact Gaussian-expectation objectives.
our_method: Using the same criterion and candidate set, we add moves that relocate all replications of a treatment together. This avoids temporarily losing pure-error degrees of freedom when moving replicates one at a time. Each start also includes perturbations of strengths 2, 3, and 4, followed by local reoptimization and retention of better designs.

The baseline and our method share low-rank updates, the initial-design stream, and the full number of starts, with final scoring under the original criterion. Group exchanges and perturbations jointly introduce new search neighborhoods, but have not been separately ablated. Extra local searches increase actual runtime; the same time limit does not imply equal computational work.
papers.baseline_implementation: Point exchange is reconstructed from the published article and author supplementary code, retaining 100 or 150 starts and correcting fixed-center initialization and rank checks. Both methods use the same accelerated implementation. The source code's prior approximation is not replaced with another objective.

experiments.label: Unblocked five-factor determinant design
experiments.setup: Allocate 40 runs among 243 three-level treatments for five factors. The primary quadratic model has 21 terms, with 30 potentially omitted terms. Use prior scales τ² = 1 and 1/30, equal weights for the three criteria, 100 shared starts, and six paired seeds.
experiments.metric: Geometric mean of composite criteria at two prior scales
experiments.explanation: The outcome is an AI win, but the gain is small. Parameter precision and mean squared error improve, while the lack-of-fit component worsens slightly, illustrating tradeoffs within the composite objective. Within each run, take the geometric mean of the criteria at the two τ² values, then the arithmetic mean across six runs. Lower is better.

experiments.label: Unblocked five-factor trace-criterion design
experiments.setup: Retain 40 runs, five three-level factors, and the same primary and omitted terms, but use trace-based precision and error criteria. Linear and interaction terms have weights 4/65, and squared terms 1/65. Use the same two τ² values, 100 starts, and six paired seeds.

The result supports the combined search but does not distinguish the contributions of group moves and perturbations. Geometrically combine the two prior scales within each run, then calculate the mean and paired differences over six repetitions.

results_interpretation: All three experiments are wins under the prespecified criteria. The trace-criterion gain is clearer; the other two gains are small. The results suggest value in jointly searching replication structure and local perturbations. Our method takes approximately 2.5–3 times as long as the baseline, and the evidence establishes neither global optimality nor an advantage at equal actual runtime.
theory: Exact low-rank updates and descent over finite neighborhoods support implementation correctness, but conservative lower bounds cannot certify global optimality. Supplementary analysis shows that a point prior with a shared positive or negative sign is not equivalent to the general Gaussian trace expectation. This correction does not alter the prespecified objective in the formal comparison.
