papers.title: Strata Design for Variance Reduction in Stochastic Simulation
papers.short_title: Adaptive rare-event probability estimation in stochastic simulation
papers.authors: Jaeshin Park; Eunshin Byon; Young Myoung Ko; Sara Shashaani
papers.research_question: Under Gaussian random inputs and noisy simulation outputs, a failure event may have a probability of only about one percent, making direct Monte Carlo costly. This paper uses historical input–output records to construct sampling strata and estimate failure probability under a fixed simulation budget, comparing learned stratification with weighted residual sampling.
intro_notes: Classification: the report retains the initial big-data subsampling category. Full-text review reassigns it to optimization, with active learning and sequential design as an overlapping category.
original_method: The original OptiTreeStrat method estimates conditional failure probabilities by kernel smoothing, proposes splits from stationary equations for stratified variance, and sequentially selects variables and splits to reduce predicted estimation variance. Independent historical subsets and resampling tests control tree complexity.

The final estimate weights within-stratum failure proportions by known stratum probabilities, allocating simulations by the Neyman principle. The present comparison retains these mechanisms while correcting conditional-variance, Gaussian-tail, and integer-allocation issues in the source implementation. The target is failure probability over the full Gaussian input domain.
our_method: We fit a radial basis function surrogate to the same historical continuous responses, then map its predicted response and residual scale to an approximate failure probability. A gridded proposal adapts only the two most influential coordinates and mixes in 10% of the original input distribution, ensuring full-domain support and controlled importance weights.

New simulations estimate the weighted residual between the failure indicator and surrogate probability, adding back the surrogate integral calculated from independent Sobol inputs. Categorical sampling from the proposal is further stratified into equal-probability groups. Five batches are combined with fixed sample-count weights, without clipping the final estimate. Even with an inaccurate surrogate, the weighted correction has explicit unbiasedness conditions.
papers.baseline_implementation: The equation-guided stratification tree is reconstructed from the author working manuscript and code, correcting issues including treating a second moment as a standard deviation and truncating Gaussian tails to a finite trial box. The comparator is the corrected full-domain baseline, not original table scores or uncorrected code.

experiments.label: Failure probability for a nonlinear three-dimensional response
experiments.setup: Inputs are three independent standard normal variables. Output noise has standard deviation 1, and the failure threshold is 17.9. The total budget is 1,200 calls. Sensitivity checks for reference-probability error preserve the conclusion, but surrogate and stratification contributions have not been separated. The nominal 340-point initial orthogonal array actually has 338 points, with the remaining calls split into five batches. Use 40 paired seeds.
experiments.metric: Mean squared error of probability estimates
experiments.explanation: Our method substantially improves this sparse high-dimensional example, with both experiments exceeding the prespecified tolerance. This does not establish equal effectiveness for every ten-dimensional function or dense interaction structure. The primary score is mean squared error across 40 probability estimates. The original paper reports the standard deviation of 100 estimates, so percentages cannot be compared directly between these statistics.

Sensitivity checks for reference-probability error preserve the conclusion, but surrogate and stratification contributions have not been separated. Take the arithmetic mean over 40 squared differences between estimated and reference probabilities. The standard deviation of probability estimates differs from that of squared errors.

Experiment 2: Our method substantially improves this sparse high-dimensional example, with both experiments exceeding the prespecified tolerance. This does not establish equal effectiveness for every ten-dimensional function or dense interaction structure. The primary score is mean squared error across 40 probability estimates. The original paper reports the standard deviation of 100 estimates, so percentages cannot be compared directly between these statistics.
results_interpretation: Both experiments are AI wins, reducing mean squared error by roughly 90% or more and also lowering the standard deviation of probability estimates. The results support combining a continuous-response surrogate, importance-weighted residual correction, and proposal stratification on these two problems. They are not percentage reductions in the standard deviations reported in the original table, and do not identify each component's individual contribution.
theory: Under full-domain support, independent fresh-batch random numbers, an independent unbiased surrogate integral, and fixed batch weights, cancellation between the surrogate integral and weighted residual gives conditional unbiasedness. The non-increasing stratification-variance result is relative only to independent sampling with the same frozen surrogate and proposal; it does not establish universal superiority over the original stratification tree.
limitations: The formal experiments use fewer repetitions than the original paper. The wind-turbine simulation was not run because required configurations were missing and computational demands were high. The proposal adapts only two coordinates, and dense high-dimensional problems remain untested. Independent quasi-Monte Carlo integration adds variance. The paper is substantively about stratified probability estimation and active sampling. Its initial Category 8 assignment differs from the original review's Category 3 assignment with Category 6 overlap.

papers.title: Gibbs Optimal Design of Experiments
papers.short_title: Loss-driven Gibbs optimal experimental design
papers.authors: Antony M. Overstall; Jacinta Holloway-Brown; James M. McGree
papers.research_question: When a full likelihood cannot be specified reliably, a task-specific loss can define a Gibbs posterior, and a designer distribution can evaluate experiments. This paper studies selecting finitely many observation locations to improve target-parameter posterior log density or squared error, while handling replication, variance calibration, and model mismatch.
original_method: The original method updates the prior through exponential loss weights, then averages design utility over responses and hyperparameters under the designer distribution. Squared response loss yields a D-type objective corrected for pure-error degrees of freedom. GP-integrated loss and count quasi-likelihood loss use approximate posteriors and Monte Carlo evaluation.

Optimization uses approximate coordinate exchange: a one-dimensional GP emulator proposes promising coordinate changes, followed by stochastic acceptance comparisons and whole-point exchanges. The target itself may depend on the design. In particular, integrated loss uses an approximate target, not exact posterior risk for a known true parameter.
our_method: For the analytic response-surface objective, we jointly optimize support locations and integer replication counts, using log-determinant gradients and multiple starts across different support sizes. This avoids breaking replication structure with individual point moves. For stochastic objectives, common random numbers screen groups of candidates, followed by independent paired samples for candidate selection.

The GP problem retains a full-rank quadratic response surface and allows replicated support points. A previously discovered rank-deficient scheme that inflated the objective is excluded from the formal method. Both methods share exact tensorization of the 1,000-node quadrature and stable calibration, so these common accelerations are not advantages unique to our method.
papers.baseline_implementation: Coordinate exchange is independently reconstructed from the 29-page arXiv v2 and the general acebayes software structure, retaining genuine GP proposals and stochastic acceptance. The original experimental program was not obtained. Leave-one-out fitting details and the count-posterior prior follow prespecified supplementary conventions.

experiments.label: Corrected D-type utility for a quadratic response surface
experiments.setup: Allocate 16 runs in [-1, 1]³ and fit the full 10-term quadratic model including an intercept. Exact replication determines pure-error degrees of freedom, with d > 2 required. Five paired seeds start from identical designs, with a 110-second search limit per run and analytic scoring.
experiments.explanation: All five pairs improve. Every final improved design has 10 support points and six pure-error degrees of freedom. Average actual runtime is longer, and global optimality is unproved. Take the arithmetic mean of five analytic objective values. Use absolute log-score differences; mechanical percentages do not represent design efficiency.

experiments.label: Utility under GP-integrated loss
experiments.setup: Again use 16 runs and a three-dimensional, 10-term model. Designer and predictive GPs have different kernels, and quadrature uses 10³ nodes. Score each design pair on 2,048 new simulated datasets, including leave-one-out fitting for each dataset. Use five paired seeds and a 360-second search limit.
experiments.metric: Mean posterior log density at the approximate target
experiments.explanation: All five pairs improve, with similar actual runtimes. This result concerns the fitted GP and delta-method approximate target; it does not establish a general advantage in learning the full response surface. Average 2,048 log densities within each run, then average over five runs. Report absolute differences, not percentage efficiency.

experiments.label: Target error for overdispersed counts
experiments.setup: Plan 50 observations in [-1, 1]² for a three-term model. Negative-binomial responses include random treatment effects, with dispersion parameter distributed as U(1, 5). Five paired seeds were planned, each evaluated on 8,192 new samples using a Poisson-projection target and Pearson calibration.
experiments.metric: Squared error of the target parameter
experiments.explanation: All-zero or separated counts prevent existence of the required unpenalized Poisson estimate. Thirteen validation samples have already failed; this cannot be attributed to a win by either optimizer. Required calibration is undefined for some samples. There is no complete formal objective value, so this experiment remains non-comparable.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 1: All five pairs improve. Every final improved design has 10 support points and six pure-error degrees of freedom. Average actual runtime is longer, and global optimality is unproved. Take the arithmetic mean of five analytic objective values. Use absolute log-score differences; mechanical percentages do not represent design efficiency.

Experiment 2: All five pairs improve, with similar actual runtimes. This result concerns the fitted GP and delta-method approximate target; it does not establish a general advantage in learning the full response surface. Average 2,048 log densities within each run, then average over five runs. Report absolute differences, not percentage efficiency.

Experiment 3: All-zero or separated counts prevent existence of the required unpenalized Poisson estimate. Thirteen validation samples have already failed; this cannot be attributed to a win by either optimizer. Required calibration is undefined for some samples. There is no complete formal objective value, so this experiment remains non-comparable.
results_interpretation: Both comparable experiments are wins, with positive differences in all five pairs. The third remains non-comparable because the required estimator is not guaranteed to exist. The analytic task uses more actual time, while runtimes are similar for the stochastic task. Conclusions are limited to the stated loss and calibration conventions; ratios of log scores cannot summarize percentage gains.
theory: A finite expectation of the inverse residual sum of squares requires d > 2, correcting an insufficient condition in the source. Exact gradients and quadrature identities support computational correctness. All-zero counts have positive probability, explaining calibration failure. Variance reduction from common random numbers additionally requires positive covariance, and loose upper bounds do not certify global optimality.
limitations: The baseline is a source-grounded independent reconstruction. Equivalence with the journal version and the authors' specific leave-one-out settings is unverified. The count experiment was not formally run. Its Gibbs prior is a supplementary convention, and its approximate projection target is not directly equivalent to a general weighted-loss target.

papers.title: Optimal designs for regression on Lie groups
papers.short_title: Equal-weight optimal designs for band-limited regression on compact Lie groups
papers.authors: Somnath Chakraborty; Holger Dette; Martin Kroll
papers.research_question: For regression on rotations, orientations, and spherical directions, geometric symmetry of the input space can determine the information matrix. This paper studies finite equal-weight observations that exactly reproduce the information of the uniform distribution for a complete band-limited regression model, and compares numerical catalogs with explicit algebraic constructions at the same observation count.
original_method: The original method uses complete blocks of Laplacian eigenfunctions as regression bases, normalized by Haar probability measure. Symmetry gives the uniform design an identity information matrix and corresponding optimality. A finite equal-weight point set attains the same information matrix if it integrates all products of basis functions exactly.

Specific designs use point sets from catalogs on the three-dimensional sphere, antipodal projections to the rotation group, and Cartesian products of spherical and rotation designs. The paper covers several optimality criteria. The primary metric here is full-model E-efficiency, the smallest eigenvalue of the normalized information matrix.
our_method: For the 97-point SU(2) catalog design, we replace generic trust-region refinement with damped tangent-space moment repair, preserving point count, unit length, and equal weights. For SO(3), we explicitly generate 12 tetrahedral rotations. For the product space, we combine a known algebraic 14-point spherical construction with these rotations.

Explicit constructions allow direct checks of low-order moments and reduce catalog reading and numerical optimization. The 14-point spherical design and tetrahedral rotations are known constructions; our contribution is implementation and proof checking. Moment repair accepts only residual reductions, which guarantees neither an E-efficiency increase at every step nor global convergence from arbitrary initial points.
papers.baseline_implementation: The complete orthogonal bases and catalog constructions are independently implemented from the 26-page arXiv v1, correcting signs in the covering map. Because the original 97-point catalog lacks sufficient precision, the baseline refines it anew in each run; this is a disclosed precision reconstruction. A weaker grid is not substituted as the baseline.

experiments.label: A 55-parameter design on SU(2)
experiments.setup: Represent SU(2) as the unit three-dimensional sphere in four-dimensional space. Use all harmonics of degrees 0–4, totaling 55 coefficients, with 97 fixed equal-weight observations. Both methods start from the same public 8-design catalog. Use five paired repetitions and a 180-second limit per run.
experiments.explanation: Both methods reach the identity information matrix to numerical precision, so the primary metric ties. Our construction takes less time, but tiny eigenvalue differences have no scientific improvement meaning. Five runs repeat the same deterministic design. Zero SD and degenerate intervals describe computational repeatability, not uncertainty from new data.

experiments.label: A 10-parameter rotation design on SO(3)
experiments.setup: Retain Wigner orders 0 and 1 on SO(3), totaling 10 coefficients, with 12 fixed equal-weight rotations. The baseline projects antipodal pairs of a 24-point spherical design; our method constructs rotations explicitly. Use five paired repetitions, a 180-second limit, and recompute six grid diagnostics.
experiments.explanation: Both 12-point designs attain E-efficiency 1 within floating-point error, giving a tie. Convenient explicit rotations do not constitute discovery of an optimal design with fewer points. There are five deterministic repetitions. Supplementary grids have 12–600 observations and do not enter the primary comparison of the two equal-weight designs.

experiments.label: A 90-parameter design on the sphere–rotation product
experiments.setup: Retain spherical degrees 0–2 and rotation orders 0–1. The complete tensor model has 90 coefficients, with 14 × 12 = 168 fixed observations. Use the same five paired repetitions and 180-second limit, additionally recomputing grids with 3,456, 12,800, and 36,000 points.
experiments.explanation: Both product designs attain numerical optimality and tie, while the algebraic construction is faster. The experiment compares information matrices only and does not establish real biological binding or predictive effects. Five repetitions are deterministic. The spherical product space uses the product measure and complete model; scoring does not use actual biological prediction errors.

results_notes: Values are means ± sample standard deviations; n is the number of paired repetitions. A positive gain favors our method. 95% intervals use the paired Student-t method.

Experiment 1: Both methods reach the identity information matrix to numerical precision, so the primary metric ties. Our construction takes less time, but tiny eigenvalue differences have no scientific improvement meaning. Five runs repeat the same deterministic design. Zero SD and degenerate intervals describe computational repeatability, not uncertainty from new data.

Experiment 2: Both 12-point designs attain E-efficiency 1 within floating-point error, giving a tie. Convenient explicit rotations do not constitute discovery of an optimal design with fewer points. There are five deterministic repetitions. Supplementary grids have 12–600 observations and do not enter the primary comparison of the two equal-weight designs.

Experiment 3: Both product designs attain numerical optimality and tie, while the algebraic construction is faster. The experiment compares information matrices only and does not establish real biological binding or predictive effects. Five repetitions are deterministic. The spherical product space uses the product measure and complete model; scoring does not use actual biological prediction errors.
results_interpretation: All three experiments tie because both methods already attain the theoretical E-efficiency upper bound. The contributions are mainly explicit constructions, shorter local construction times, and moment proofs that are easier to check. Neither model size nor sample count is reduced, and repeated execution adds no independent scientific samples.
theory: For compact connected Lie groups with a bi-invariant metric, an existing spectral-localization mechanism gives a product-frequency bound, tightening the paper's general sufficient condition from 14Λ to 4Λ. This is neither a claim of first discovery nor a minimum-point theorem, and does not apply to arbitrary metrics. The three experiments already use finer truncations and do not reduce sample counts through this result.
limitations: Floating-point refinement of the 97-point design is not a rigorous interval certificate. Catalog coordinates actually move, so the change cannot be described as output rounding alone. Equivalence between journal and preprint versions and the authors' grid-endpoint details is unverified. The historical 225-point rounding comparison was not run. Existing constructions and spectral mechanisms retain their literature attribution. Runtime reflects only the local implementation and excludes external catalog-generation costs.
